1. PURPOSE. This CONPLAN translates JSCP tasking (Ref a) into an operational concept for a time-bound, notional multi-domain joint integration exercise in INDOPACOM’s Western Pacific area of responsibility, with baseline conditions of contested logistics, persistent EMS/cyber contestation, and degraded/intermittent space-enabled services. This plan is designed to drive realistic subordinate planning (including daily air tasking cycle inputs, joint collection management prioritization, and logistics synchronization) without providing tactical employment instructions or target-specific direction. This CONPLAN supports follow-on refinement into executable orders and supporting plans consistent with JP 5-0.

2. SITUATION.

   a. Strategic/Operational Context. From 01–08 MAR 2026, USINDOPACOM conducts MDIX to validate distributed posture, resilient C2, and sustainment under contested logistics and space coverage gaps. The adversary conducts calibrated coercion below armed conflict threshold, with rapid escalation options and a mature long-range precision strike complex. The operational problem is maintaining decision advantage and credible denial while preserving force survivability and sustainment when SATCOM/PNT/ISR transport are intermittent and logistics nodes are threatened (Refs a, c, g).

   b. Adversary Capabilities (Near-Peer, Pacific).
      (1) A2/AD Threat to Access and Sustainment. Adversary fields integrated air and maritime sensors and long-range strike systems that can threaten fixed and semi-fixed nodes (ports, airfields, fuel farms, communications sites), distribution routes, and high-demand platforms. Capability includes rapid targeting of signatures, pattern-of-life exploitation, and exploitation of predictable logistics rhythms.
      (2) Counterspace and Space-Enabled Denial. Adversary possesses capabilities to disrupt or degrade SATCOM, PNT, and ISR dissemination via jamming, spoofing, cyber effects on ground segments, and localized denial. Expected effects: intermittent loss of beyond-line-of-sight communications, timing errors, navigation inaccuracies, and degraded ISR transport.
      (3) Cyber/EMS Contestation. Adversary can conduct persistent cyber reconnaissance, intrusion attempts, and disruptive attacks against mission networks, logistics IT, and operational technology; employ electronic warfare to deny or degrade tactical data links, navigation aids, and radar/communications.
      (4) Information Operations (IO). Adversary conducts influence operations to undermine coalition cohesion, amplify incidents, and drive escalation narratives; attempts to create decision paralysis through ambiguity, misinformation, and attribution challenges (Ref i).

   c. Adversary Limitations/Vulnerabilities (Planning Assumptions).
      (1) Adversary kill chain effectiveness declines with dispersion, signature reduction, and deception; targeting confidence is sensitive to ISR continuity and data integrity.
      (2) Adversary must allocate finite ISR and strike resources across multiple domains and geographic approaches; overload and misdirection can impose operational dilemmas.
      (3) Adversary IO effectiveness is constrained by timely, credible allied messaging and operational transparency consistent with policy.

   d. Friendly Forces/Capabilities Available (Notional for Exercise Planning).
      (1) USINDOPACOM Joint Force Elements (categories):
          (a) Joint Force Air Component (JFACC) capabilities: multi-role fighter aviation; air mobility; airborne C2/relay; theater air and missile defense enablers; ISR platforms; aeromedical evacuation.
          (b) Joint Force Maritime Component (JFMCC) capabilities: surface combatants; undersea warfare elements as apportioned; maritime patrol; sealift coordination; mine countermeasure planning and limited execution injects.
          (c) Joint Force Land Component (JFLCC) / Army forces: theater sustainment, movement control, integrated air and missile defense contributions, expeditionary basing and airfield opening support, port opening elements, protection and security forces for nodes and convoys.
          (d) Marine forces: expeditionary advanced base operations (EABO) planning injects; littoral operations; aviation and ground logistics contributions; base defense.
          (e) Space/Cyber: USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM coordination and space mission assurance integration; USCYBERCOM coordination for defensive cyber operations (DCO), incident response, and hunt forward–style training injects; service cyber protection teams as available.
          (f) Special Operations (as applicable): liaison, ISR integration, and theater cooperation planning; no direct-action employment is directed by this CONPLAN.
      (2) Allies/Partners. Selected allies/partners participate in MDIX through liaison officers, information-sharing rehearsal, and limited combined events as directed by standing agreements and releasability rules. Combined integration focuses on C2 interoperability, maritime domain awareness, and logistics coordination under degraded communications.

   e. Theater Geography (Western Pacific).
      (1) Operating Environment. Maritime-dominant theater with extended lines of communication, constrained airfield/port capacity, and weather-driven operating impacts. Key terrain includes dispersed islands, chokepoints, and approaches through the First and Second Island Chains. Long distances impose fuel and maintenance demands; distributed operations require multiple nodes with varying infrastructure.
      (2) Implications. Geography favors an adversary’s long-range targeting of predictable hubs; friendly success depends on dispersion, mobility, deception, redundant distribution, and resilient C2 (Refs c, f). Airspace is complex with overlapping civil/military use; joint airspace control must function under intermittent data links (Ref d).

   f. Assumptions.
      (1) Contested logistics is continuous; distribution nodes may be disrupted with little warning (Ref f).
      (2) SATCOM availability is intermittent; PNT may be locally degraded; ISR transport may be delayed or denied (Ref g).
      (3) Cyber/EMS contestation is persistent, affecting both operational and sustainment systems (Refs h, i).
      (4) Exercise is conducted below threshold of armed conflict; rules of engagement and political constraints emphasize de-escalation and defensive posturing consistent with international law.
      (5) Host-nation support and access are variable and may require rapid adaptation to policy constraints.

   g. Constraints/Restraints.
      (1) Comply with applicable policy, standing rules for the use of force, and theater authorities; protect sensitive capabilities and tactics; adhere to releasability guidance.
      (2) Ensure safety and deconfliction with civil air/maritime traffic; implement risk controls consistent with joint and component safety programs.
      (3) No target-specific strike planning is directed within this CONPLAN; effects-based demonstrations will be simulated or executed within exercise control measures.

3. MISSION STATEMENT. USINDOPACOM conducts MDIX in the Western Pacific from 01–08 MAR 2026 to validate a theater-wide distributed posture and maneuver framework, resilient C2 under intermittent SATCOM/degraded PNT, integrated air-maritime-space-cyber operations, and contested logistics sustainment—demonstrating credible denial, degrading adversary kill-chain confidence through dispersion/deception, protecting the joint force and key nodes, and sustaining operational tempo with mission-type orders and rehearsed degraded-communications battle drills (Refs a–i).

4. CONCEPT OF OPERATIONS.

   a. Commander’s Intent.
      (1) Purpose: Prove the joint force can maintain decision advantage and credible deterrence in the Western Pacific while operating dispersed and sustaining forces when space-enabled services and logistics are contested.
      (2) Method: Employ distributed posture, resilient and redundant C2 pathways (PACE), mission-type orders, rapid reconstitution, deception/signature management, and prioritized sustainment distribution. Integrate air and maritime maneuver with space/cyber mission assurance and joint airspace control measures adaptable under degraded data links (Refs b–e, g–i).
      (3) End State (Exercise): Joint force demonstrates (a) ability to disperse and operate from multiple nodes with survivability and sustainment; (b) continued execution of prioritized tasks under communications loss; (c) effective joint airspace control and dynamic coordination despite degraded ISR/SATCOM; and (d) a logistics system that continues to deliver fuel, munitions, and critical parts under disruption with measured risk.

   b. Phasing (aligned to JP 3-0 construct; execution window 01–08 MAR 2026).

      PHASE 0 — SHAPE (pre-01 MAR preparation; validated during early exercise days)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Establish baseline distributed posture framework (primary/alternate operating locations, mobility triggers, EMCON guidance).
          (b) Confirm C2 architecture with PACE communications, data prioritization, and minimum essential information requirements.
          (c) Validate logistics posture for dispersion (prepositioning, load plans, movement control, alternate distribution methods).
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Issue mission-type orders emphasizing commander’s intent, delegated authorities, and “lost comms” battle drills (Ref b).
          (b) Establish joint airspace control plan adaptable under degraded data links (Ref d).
          (c) Conduct cyber hygiene surge and incident response rehearsals; establish cyber/EMS reporting and common operational picture (COP) degradation procedures (Refs h, i).
          (d) Coordinate space mission assurance measures: alternate PNT procedures, protected SATCOM prioritization, ISR dissemination workarounds (Ref g).

      PHASE 1 — DETER (01–02 MAR)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Demonstrate credible denial posture through dispersal readiness, defensive counterair/maritime defense integration (simulated or controlled execution).
          (b) Increase adversary uncertainty by reducing signatures, varying patterns, and employing deception injects.
          (c) Confirm coalition information-sharing and decision processes under communications constraints.
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Execute dispersal drill to selected distributed operating locations (DOLs) and maritime operating areas; validate command relationships and support agreements.
          (b) Practice defensive counterair and maritime coordination with joint airspace control measures; emphasize deconfliction with civil traffic and safety (Refs d, e).
          (c) Run “degraded SATCOM episode” injects to force transition to alternate C2 pathways and offline workflows.
          (d) Establish logistics distribution rhythm with variability; test movement control under route disruptions.

      PHASE 2 — SEIZE INITIATIVE (03–05 MAR)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Maintain operational tempo while space and cyber conditions deteriorate; demonstrate mission continuation with partial COP and delayed ISR.
          (b) Degrade adversary kill-chain confidence via dispersion, deception, and rapid reconstitution of disrupted nodes.
          (c) Validate cross-domain coordination among air, maritime, land, space, and cyber components with disciplined data prioritization.
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Conduct joint C2 resilience drills: transition between primary and alternate C2 nodes; practice “minimum essential information” reporting.
          (b) Execute integrated air-maritime events (simulated effects) requiring joint targeting coordination processes without reliance on continuous ISR feeds; validate time-sensitive coordination procedures at a conceptual level (Ref e).
          (c) Conduct logistics “shock” injects: loss of a primary node; fuel/munitions shortfall; cyber disruption to logistics IT; require re-routing, substitution, and prioritization (Ref f).
          (d) Exercise joint personnel recovery coordination (staff-level) under intermittent comms.

      PHASE 3 — DOMINATE (06–07 MAR)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Demonstrate ability to concentrate effects from dispersed positions while sustaining force protection and deconfliction.
          (b) Demonstrate theater sustainment endurance through redundancy and protected distribution.
          (c) Validate that joint airspace control and ATO/ACO processes remain viable with data link degradation and reduced SATCOM.
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Conduct a major joint integration event: combined air and maritime maneuver with space/cyber injects, emphasizing C2 discipline and safety (Refs c–e).
          (b) Execute reconstitution drills: repair/restoration of a degraded node, reallocation of sorties/maritime tasks, redistribution of sustainment.
          (c) Conduct information operations synchronization: proactive, truthful messaging; counter-misinformation drill; coalition narrative alignment (Ref i).

      PHASE 4 — STABILIZE (08 MAR and immediate post-exercise transition)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Transition to steady-state posture; capture lessons learned and capability gaps.
          (b) Produce prioritized observations for doctrine, training, materiel, leadership/education, personnel, facilities, and policy (DOTMLPF-P).

      (2) Key Tasks:

          (c) Issue follow-on planning guidance for supporting plans and capability submissions.

   c. Lines of Operation (LOO) (mutually supporting; assessed daily).

      LOO 1 — Distributed Posture & Maneuver (DENY)
      - Establish and sustain dispersed operating posture across air/maritime/land nodes; validate rapid dispersion and controlled concentration triggers; reduce predictability via variable patterns and EMCON.

      LOO 2 — Resilient Command and Control (DEGRADE/PROTECT)
      - Maintain effective decision-making with intermittent SATCOM and partial COP using PACE communications, mission-type orders, data prioritization, and offline workflows; validate cross-domain coordination and delegated authorities (Refs b, c, g).

      LOO 3 — Integrated Airspace Control & Air Operations (DENY/PROTECT)
      - Ensure safe, effective joint airspace control (ACO/ACP execution) under degraded data links; maintain deconfliction, ID procedures, and priority of air defense tasks (Refs d, e).

      LOO 4 — Contested Logistics & Sustainment (SUSTAIN/PROTECT)
      - Sustain operations with redundant distribution methods, dispersed stocks, rapid reroute, and protected movement control; maintain fuel, munitions, and critical parts delivery despite disruptions (Ref f).

      LOO 5 — Protection, Signature Management & Deception (PROTECT/DEGRADE)
      - Reduce vulnerability of nodes and platforms through integrated base defense, mobility, camouflage/concealment, emissions discipline, decoys (exercise-simulated), and rapid reconstitution planning.

      LOO 6 — Space/Cyber Mission Assurance & Information Resilience (DEGRADE)
      - Integrate space mission assurance measures; execute defensive cyber operations and incident response; sustain trusted information flows and counter adversary misinformation (Refs g–i).

   d. Decisive Points (exercise-defined conditions that determine success of the operational approach).
      (1) DP1: Joint force successfully transitions from steady-state communications to alternate C2 (PACE) within defined time standards while maintaining safe airspace control and mission continuity (Refs b, d).
      (2) DP2: Sustained sortie/maritime task generation continues after loss or degradation of a primary logistics node through redistribution and prioritization without unsafe degradation of operations (Ref f).
      (3) DP3: Joint airspace control remains effective during data link degradation (fallback ID procedures, altitude blocks, procedural control) while maintaining civil deconfliction (Ref d).
      (4) DP4: Coalition information-sharing continues under releasability constraints and comms degradation using preplanned products, release procedures, and liaison networks.
      (5) DP5: Cyber incident response contains and restores mission-essential functions within acceptable time, with validated manual/alternate processes for logistics and C2 (Ref h).
      (6) DP6: Space degradation injects (PNT/SATCOM/ISR transport) do not halt decision cycles; alternate nav/timing and reporting procedures are executed effectively (Ref g).

5. ADVERSARY COURSES OF ACTION (COA) (notional for exercise inject design).

   COA 1 — “Gray-Zone Pressure with Precision ISR”
   - Adversary uses maritime and air presence, IO narratives, and cyber probing to create ambiguity; applies localized jamming and intermittent SATCOM disruption to stress C2; conducts aggressive ISR to map dispersed nodes and logistics patterns. Intended effect: deter friendly maneuver, force consolidation, and induce political friction.

   COA 2 — “Kill-Chain Acceleration Against Logistics”
   - Adversary prioritizes disruption of sustainment: cyber effects on logistics IT, EW against navigation/port operations, and simulated long-range strike threats against predictable hubs. Intended effect: create fuel/munitions shortfalls, slow operational tempo, and compel risk acceptance or withdrawal.

   COA 3 — “Space-Enabled C2 Disruption with IO Amplification”
   - Adversary degrades SATCOM and PNT locally while amplifying misinformation regarding incidents and alleged escalation. Intended effect: fragment coalition decision-making, slow authorization cycles, and undermine confidence in data integrity.

6. FRIENDLY COURSES OF ACTION (RECOMMENDED COA).

   COA R — “Distributed Resilience with Controlled Concentration”
   a. Summary. Employ a dispersed posture with mission-type orders and robust PACE communications; prioritize sustainment dispersion and protected distribution; operate joint airspace control with procedural fallbacks; integrate space/cyber mission assurance; and selectively concentrate effects (simulated/demonstrative) when decisive points require, then rapidly re-disperse to reduce targetability.

   b. Why COA R. This approach directly implements JSCP priorities (DENY/DEGRADE/PROTECT/SUSTAIN) under baseline degraded space and contested logistics, while minimizing single-point dependencies and enabling continued operations with partial information (Refs a–i).

   c. Risk and Mitigation.
      (1) Risk: Reduced efficiency due to dispersion and procedural airspace control. Mitigation: preplanned airspace control measures, rehearsed battle drills, and minimum essential coordination procedures (Refs d, e).
      (2) Risk: Logistics shortfalls from disrupted distribution. Mitigation: prepositioned stocks, alternate distribution, prioritized consumption controls, and movement control redundancy (Ref f).
      (3) Risk: COP degradation increases fratricide/safety hazard. Mitigation: strict ID and procedural control measures, clear ROE/standing guidance, and conservative deconfliction (Ref d).
      (4) Risk: Cyber compromise of sustainment/C2 systems. Mitigation: DCO posture, segmentation, manual fallback processes, and incident response rehearsals (Ref h).

8. LOGISTICS CONCEPT (JP 4-0 aligned; designed for contested logistics conditions).

   a. Logistics Intent. Sustain distributed joint operations during MDIX by designing logistics to be survivable, redundant, and adaptable: disperse stocks; vary distribution patterns; prioritize mission-essential requirements; and enable rapid reroute and reconstitution when nodes are degraded or denied.

      (2) Component commanders (JFMCC, JFACC, JFLCC, MARFORPAC) execute assigned tasks and provide forces/capabilities per allocation; coordinate through joint boards, centers, and working groups.
      (3) Space and cyber coordination occurs through established support relationships: USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM integrates space mission assurance; USCYBERCOM coordination for DCO/IR alignment and deconfliction (Refs g, h).

   b. C2 Architecture and PACE Communications.
      (1) Primary: SATCOM-enabled joint networks and standard operational COP services (acknowledged intermittent).
      (2) Alternate: Line-of-sight networks, terrestrial relays, and airborne gateways; procedural reporting formats for ATO/ACO essential coordination.
      (3) Contingency: Low-bandwidth data paths, store-and-forward messaging, scheduled windows, and courier-assisted transfer where feasible.

   b. (U//FOUO) Operational Environment.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Geography and Distance. The Western Pacific theater is maritime-dominant with extended lines of communication (LOCs), a limited number of high-capacity ports and airfields, and significant weather variability. Joint force success depends on dispersion, mobility, deception, redundant distribution, and resilient command and control (C2). Long-range mobility and sustainment demands (fuel, maintenance, munitions, medical) are decisive constraints (JP 4-0).
      (2) (U//FOUO) Civil Considerations. Airspace and sea lanes include dense civil traffic requiring disciplined joint airspace control measures and maritime deconfliction, particularly during communications degradation. Host-nation and access permissions vary by location and are subject to exercise control (EXCON) policy injects.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Space/Cyber/EMS Conditions. Exercise conditions include intermittent SATCOM availability, localized PNT degradation, variable ISR transport latency, and persistent cyber/EMS contestation affecting both operational and sustainment systems (JP 3-14, JP 3-12). These conditions will be introduced via controlled injects, with safety-of-flight protections and pre-coordinated risk controls.

   c. (U//FOUO) Adversary (Near-Peer State, Pacific). A near-peer state adversary (OPFOR) conducts calibrated coercion below the armed conflict threshold, with rapid escalation options.       (1) (U//FOUO) A2/AD Threat to Access and Sustainment. OPFOR can threaten fixed and semi-fixed nodes (ports, airfields, fuel storage, communications sites) and distribution routes, exploiting predictable logistics rhythms, signatures, and pattern-of-life.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Counterspace and Space-Enabled Denial. OPFOR can disrupt SATCOM and degrade PNT and ISR dissemination through jamming/spoofing and cyber effects against ground/transport segments, producing intermittent BLOS loss, timing errors, and navigation inaccuracies.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Cyber/EMS Contestation. OPFOR conducts persistent cyber reconnaissance and disruptive attempts against mission networks, logistics IT (including movement and inventory management), and operational technology; simultaneously contests tactical data links and navigation aids.
      (4) (U//FOUO) Information Operations. OPFOR seeks to undermine coalition cohesion and induce decision paralysis through misinformation, narrative framing, and attribution ambiguity.

2. (U//FOUO) MISSION.

USINDOPACOM conducts MDIX in the Western Pacific from 01–08 MAR 2026 to validate theater-wide distributed posture and maneuver, resilient C2 under intermittent SATCOM and degraded PNT, integrated air–maritime–space–cyber operations, and contested logistics sustainment—demonstrating credible denial, degrading adversary kill-chain confidence through dispersion/deception, protecting the joint force and key nodes, and sustaining operational tempo with mission-type orders and rehearsed degraded-communications battle drills.

   c. (U//FOUO) Land / Expeditionary / Sustainment Forces Required.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Theater Sustainment Command (TSC)-equivalent headquarters capability to run distribution, movement control, and sustainment synchronization under JP 4-0.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Expeditionary airfield and port opening elements sufficient to activate, operate, and then displace at multiple nodes during the exercise, including material handling equipment, fuel distribution, and limited runway/port services.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Protection forces for base defense and convoy security training injects, including CBRN readiness and medical response elements.

   d. (U//FOUO) Space/Cyber Forces Required.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Space coordination teams to provide daily space support estimates, mission assurance, and incident response linkages.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Defensive cyber protection teams to support hunt, incident response, and restoration drills focused on mission and logistics networks.

6. (U//FOUO) LOGISTICS (JP 4-0).

   a. (U//FOUO) Logistics Intent. Sustain distributed operations for seven days under persistent disruption while demonstrating the ability to (1) prioritize limited lift, (2) re-route around disrupted nodes, (3) operate without full digital logistics systems, and (4) maintain readiness through disciplined consumption and maintenance recovery.

   b. (U//FOUO) Concept of Support.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Priorities of Sustainment (generic order; JTF may adjust daily): (1) aviation and maritime fuel; (2) critical spares and munitions (training allocations); (3) medical and personnel support; (4) communications/cyber restoration materials; (5) base life support.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Distribution. Use a hub-and-spoke concept with multiple small spokes and pre-identified alternates. Exercise will include controlled injects that force closure or degradation of a primary node; logistics will respond via alternate nodes, split loads, variable timing, and alternate modes (air, sea, intra-theater surface).
      (3) (U//FOUO) Contested Logistics Battle Drills. Each component will rehearse: rapid reallocation of stocks; manual reporting when logistics IT is degraded; convoy/airlift mission re-planning under comms loss; and cross-servicing agreements for fuel and limited spares.
      (4) (U//FOUO) Maintenance and Readiness. Emphasize forward maintenance capability sized for dispersed operations (minimal essential test equipment, cannibalization controls, and fly-away kits). Measure readiness recovery after displacement and comm/cyber events.
      (5) (U//FOUO) Medical. Establish distributed Role 1/Role 2 coverage commensurate with exercise events; plan for aeromedical evacuation under comms degradation using pre-briefed routing and patient movement requests via alternate channels.
      (6) (U//FOUO) Contracting and Host-Nation Support. J4 coordinates contracting/host-nation support per permissions. Exercise includes injects that reduce contracted support to force adaptation and internal capability use.
      (7) (U//FOUO) Reporting. J4 publishes a daily sustainment SITREP format with a manual fallback. Metrics include: time-to-redirect shipment; time-to-restore minimum comms; fuel days-of-supply by node (coarse bands); sortie sustainment impacts; and maintenance turnaround.

   c. (U//FOUO) Risk Management. Logistics operations will balance dispersion with safety and force protection. Where comms degradation increases navigation or airfield/port risk, commanders will adopt conservative thresholds and use procedural control measures. EXCON retains authority to pause events for safety.

7. (U//FOUO) COMMAND AND CONTROL (JP 3-0; JP 3-30; JP 3-52; JP 3-12; JP 3-14).

   a. (U//FOUO) Command Relationships.
      (1) (U//FOUO) CDRUSINDOPACOM exercises COCOM through JTF-MDIX (exercise construct). Functional components (JFACC, JFMCC, JFLCC, JFSOCC) are established for MDIX with supporting/supporting relationships specified in the EXORD and component orders.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Supported Commander for Airspace Control. JFACC is designated Airspace Control Authority (ACA) for MDIX execution unless otherwise directed; JFMCC and JFLCC support with airspace coordination requirements (JP 3-52).
      (3) (U//FOUO) Cyber/Space Coordination. USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM provides space coordination and mission assurance; cyber forces provide DCO support. Coordination occurs through established cells embedded in the JTF battle rhythm.

   b. (U//FOUO) C2 Concept (Resilient Mission Command).
      (1) (U//FOUO) PACE Communications Plan. The JTF employs layered communications pathways: primary digital/SATCOM; alternate terrestrial networks (where available) and HF; contingency line-of-sight relay via airborne/ground assets; emergency courier/read-back procedures and pre-briefed execution matrices. Components will rehearse transition triggers and restoration procedures daily.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Degraded-Communications Battle Drills. Each component maintains a comm-out checklist: (a) execute last lawful order for a defined period; (b) shift to pre-briefed decision matrix; (c) attempt recontact via alternate; (d) report status upon restoration. These drills are validated through EXCON injects.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Battle Rhythm. Daily cycle includes: JTF update brief; JSM; ATO/ACO coordination events; LSB; cyber/space synchronization huddle; and end-of-day assessment. During comms outages, the JTF uses pre-scheduled windows and procedural check-ins.

   c. (U//FOUO) Information Management / Knowledge Management.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Establish minimum essential information set (MEIS) for degraded operations: friendly posture status bands, logistics status bands, airspace control changes, safety notices, and CCIR.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Implement releasability controls for allied/partner sharing; provide “sanitized common operating picture” products when full ISR feeds are unavailable.

   d. (U//FOUO) Assessment and Reporting.
      (1) (U//FOUO) J7 leads assessment with measures tied to end state: comms outage resilience, logistics reroute time, airspace control continuity, cross-domain coordination quality, and cyber/space incident response timeliness.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Capture capability/interoperability gaps suitable for CJCSI 3170.01 pathways, including urgent cross-domain data standards, manual fallback training gaps, and logistics IT resilience shortfalls.

8. (U//FOUO) COORDINATING INSTRUCTIONS.

   a. (U//FOUO) Safety and Deconfliction. All components comply with EXCON safety controls, range regulations, and civil deconfliction requirements. When in doubt, safety overrides training objectives.

   b. (U//FOUO) OPSEC. Do not disseminate sensitive movement or posture details beyond authorized channels. Use approved exercise cover terms where applicable.

   c. (U//FOUO) Legal/Policy. Ensure operations conform to SRUF, host-nation restrictions, and applicable law. Cyber and information activities remain defensive and exercise-authorized.

   d. (U//FOUO) Environmental and Navigational Compliance. Maritime and air operations comply with environmental rules and safe navigation practices; no exercise activity will create real-world hazards to navigation or civil aviation.

9. (U//FOUO) ADMINISTRATION AND LOGISTICS (Administrative).

   a. (U//FOUO) Personnel Accountability. Components report daily personnel accountability status through established channels, with manual backup during IT outages.

   b. (U//FOUO) Medical Reporting. Report incidents and medical events per theater medical SOP. Exercise includes simulated mass casualty injects; real-world response remains primary.

   c. (U//FOUO) Public Affairs. All public release coordinated through JTF PAO and consistent with approved themes/messages; counter-misinformation responses coordinated with information activities cell per JP 3-13.

10. (U//FOUO) COMMAND.

   a. (U//FOUO) Command Posts. JTF maintains primary and alternate C2 nodes with COOP procedures; components identify alternate nodes and minimal manning for continuity.

   b. (U//FOUO) Succession of Command. As published in JTF-MDIX EXORD and component orders.

11. (U//FOUO) SUMMARY.

This OPLAN provides operational-level direction to execute MDIX 01–08 MAR 2026 in INDOPACOM’s Western Pacific theater to validate distributed posture, resilient C2 under degraded space services, integrated joint air-maritime-space-cyber operations, and contested logistics sustainment. Components will execute phased objectives, prioritize safety and policy compliance, and capture lessons learned and capability gaps consistent with JP 5-0 and CJCSI 3170.01 pathways.

SPECIAL INSTRUCTIONS (SPINS)
INDOPACOM — WESTERN PACIFIC
MULTI-DOMAIN INTEGRATION EXERCISE (MDIX) / OPERATION INDOPACOM SHIELD
EFFECTIVE: 01–08 MAR 2026

PURPOSE: These Special Instructions (SPINS) provide standardized, theater-level operating procedures, restrictions, frequencies, and deconfliction measures to enable safe, coordinated, and resilient multi-domain operations in the Western Pacific MDIX window. All units, components, and combined/partner forces participating in MDIX shall comply with these SPINS. These instructions implement and are traceable to the NDS Extract (01 MAR 2026), NMS Theater Annex (01 MAR 2026), JSCP tasking (01 MAR 2026), and INDOPACOM CONPLAN/OPLAN (Operation INDOPACOM SHIELD). This document is UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO.

CONTENTS:
1. GENERAL (ROE, PID, CIVCAS AVERSION)
2. AIRSPACE CONTROL (ALTITUDE DECONFLICTION, RESTRICTED/CONTROLLED AREAS, ROZ/COORDINATES)
3. TANKER OPERATIONS (AIR REFUELING TRACKS, AIRCRAFT, FUEL STATES, RECOVERY PROCEDURES)
4. CSAR (ALERT POSTURE, TASKED UNITS, FREQUENCIES, RECOVERY PROCEDURES)
5. SPACE SUPPORT (GPS DEGRADATION WARNINGS, SATCOM PRIORITY, OPIR/SSA DATA FEEDS)
6. COMMUNICATIONS (PRIMARY/BACKUP FREQUENCIES, NET STRUCTURE, EMCON/ANTI-JAM PROCEDURES)

1. GENERAL
1.1 Applicability. These SPINS apply to all US forces, assigned/attached allied and partner forces, and contracted aviation participating in MDIX in the INDOPACOM Western Pacific AOR 01–08 MAR 2026. Compliance with these SPINS is mandatory; deviations must be coordinated with the applicable component Airspace Control Authority (ACA)/Joint Force Air Component (JFAC) and approved by CDRUSINDOPACOM staff J5/J3.

1.2 Rules of Engagement (ROE) & Use of Force.
  a. ROE governing MDIX are issued separately (ROE Annex A) and remain in effect. Except where explicit exercise injects alter, the baseline ROE are conservative and emphasize de-escalation consistent with the NDS Extract priorities: DENY coercive advantage, PROTECT forces and partners, and PREVENT unintended escalation.
  b. Positive Identification (PID) requirement. Positive Identification shall be established prior to the use of lethal force against any air or maritime contact unless hostile intent or hostile act is unambiguously evident. PID standards: visual ID, IFF Mode 4/5/Enhanced Mode 5 authentication, EW signature correlation, or validated intelligence cue. Units must document PID process and time-stamp evidence in mission reports.
  c. Escalation control. All engagements that could produce kinetic effects beyond self-defense require immediate report to JFC (via JOC/J3) and clearance per the escalation matrix in the ROE Annex.

1.3 Civilian Casualty Avoidance (CIVCAS).
  a. Risk Mitigation. Units will apply the law of armed conflict (LOAC) principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution. Targeting and weapons employment must consider population centers, port/harbor infrastructure, and commercial shipping lanes.
  b. Civilian objects. Ports, commercial airfields, major industrial complexes, offshore windfarms, undersea telecommunications infrastructure, and humanitarian assistance staging areas are designated protected or restricted for MDIX unless specifically released in writing by the JFC. Any planned fires, blasts, or emissions that could affect civilian mariner/air traffic require 72-hour NOTAM/NOTMAR coordination unless waived by CDRUSINDOPACOM J3.
  c. Pre- and post-strike measures. Information operations must include warnings to minimize CIVCAS where feasible. Immediate post-event battle damage assessments (BDA) shall include CIVCAS estimates and be forwarded to the JOC and HN liaison elements.

1.4 Identification, Friend or Foe (IFF).
  a. All participating aircraft will operate IFF Mode 5 and S-TTL authentication where equipment permits. Non-compliant aircraft will be restricted to corridors and require flight-following by a designated control agency.
  b. Maritime forces will operate designated AIS profiles consistent with operational security (OPSEC) guidance; AIS may be selectively withheld during deniable or contested phases—such withholding must be coordinated through the maritime component.

2. AIRSPACE CONTROL
2.1 Airspace Control System. The INDOPACOM ACA establishes an Airspace Control Order (ACO) daily. The ACO governs controlled, restricted, and advisory airspace for MDIX. The Joint Airspace Management Cell (JAMC) will publish ACO updates at H-12 and H-2 daily during MDIX; emergency updates may be released as required.

2.2 Altitude Deconfliction.
  a. All participating fixed- and rotary-wing aircraft will adhere to the altitude strata in the ACO unless specifically cleared otherwise:
     - LOW STRATA (Surface to FL150): Assigned to maritime helicopters, littoral strike craft, tactical lift (CH-53, MH-60, V-22), and some UAV BLOS denied operations.
     - MID STRATA (FL150 to FL260): Assigned to tactical fighters (F-35A/B/C, F-22), CAS, and some ISR/ELINT platforms.
     - HIGH STRATA (FL260 and above): Assigned to strategic lift, AEW (E-2D, E-3/Future), high-altitude ISR, and air-refueling tankers when operating at altitude.
  b. Vertical buffer zones. A 1,000 ft buffer above/below assigned altitude layers will be enforced for all non-emergency transit. Emergency maneuvers must be annunciated on the appropriate airspace net immediately.

2.3 Restriction/Operating Zones (ROZ) & Coordinates.
  a. All ROZ/No-Fly/Control Areas listed below are exercise specific and in effect for MDIX. Coordinates in WGS-84 (Lat/Long, decimal degrees). Times are ZULU.
     - ROZ-01 (Archipelago East Corridor): 18.5000N 144.8000E to 18.9000N 145.6000E — radius 35 NM sector; alt: SFC–FL150; active 01–08 MAR 2026 0000–2359Z. Reserved for rotary-wing CSAR and partner maritime insertion training. All overflights require ACA clearance.
     - ROZ-02 (Central Exercise Area - North): 20.2500N 150.5000E center, radius 50 NM; alt: SFC–FL260; active 02–06 MAR 0600–1800Z. Reserved for combined strike package integration; dynamic deconfliction required.
     - ROZ-03 (Central Exercise Area - South): 18.0000N 148.0000E center, radius 40 NM; alt: SFC–FL360; active 03–05 MAR 0200–2200Z. Reserved for high-altitude ISR and tanking corridors.
     - ROZ-04 (Critical Sea Line of Communication (SLOC) Cover): 16.2000N 147.5000E to 17.8000N 149.1000E box; alt: SFC–Unlimited; active 01–08 MAR 0000–2359Z; maritime and air anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) suppression demonstration area. Commercial shipping advised to transit outside or with prior coordination.
  b. Restricted Operating Zones (dynamic). Temporary ROZs (T-ROZ) will be published via ACO and broadcast on the Airspace Management Net when live fires, EW emissions, or live ship-surface gunfire are underway. T-ROZ coordinates and times will be promulgated minimum 30 minutes prior to activation, except for safety/case-of-force incidents.

2.4 Airspace Reserved for Partner/Allied Forces. Allied national air elements (e.g., PACAF-liaison collection) will be allocated corridors and altitudes per the ACO. National caveats must be honored; component ACA will annotate in daily ATO/ACO.

2.5 Deconfliction Procedures. Mission planners must coordinate via the JAMC and submit intent messages (MISSION INTENT) at H-24 and H-3. Real-time deconfliction via the Airspace Management Net is required before entering an active ROZ.

3. TANKER OPERATIONS (AIR REFUELING)

  b. Secondary AR Track S1 (South Track) — Center 18.5000N 148.5000E; track length 120 NM (NW-SE); alt FL220–FL260; bearings 135/315 true. Assigned to KC-46A and allied tanker detachments. Active 02–07 MAR 0200–2000Z.
  c. Contingency AR Holding Tracks (CHT) — allocated adjacent to ROZ-03 to enable rapid rejoin for CAP and high-altitude ISR (CHT-1 Center 19.2000N 149.0000E radius 30 NM).

3.2 Tanker Units and On-Station Procedures.
  a. Designated tanker units: 22 ARW (KC-135R), 6 ARW (KC-46A), and rotational tankers from theater-based detachments (E.g., 36 ARW). Allied tankers (e.g., RAAF KC-30A) may be integrated per SOFA/MDIX LOA.
  b. Tanker on-station fuel state (minimums). Tankers will declare minimum recovery fuel states per component Air Refueling SOP: bingo state to home base—contingent on mission; scheduled bingo for receiver planning: 8,500 lbs (KC-135), 12,000 lbs (KC-46A). Emergency fuel states must be broadcast on the Air Refueling Net and visible to receiver via pre-briefed callsigns.
  c. Aircrew Procedures. Standard ASTP or case I/II/III AR procedures per the Air Refueling Handbook apply. All receivers and tankers shall brief HOOK/RELEASE contingency procedures for ECM/jamming events.

3.3 Air Refueling Frequencies & Callsigns.
  a. Air Refueling Net (Primary): UHF LOS — 301.725 MHz AM (designated AES: ARNET-INDO-PAC A). Backup: 135.975 MHz AM.
  b. Tanker Control Callsigns: "STARLIFT-AR" (KC-135/46 organic to 5/7 AFCENT-like tasking), "BLUEARROW" (allied tankers), "JACKAL-AR" (theater rapid response).
  c. Emergency jettison/kill switch procedures. All tankers will conform to wing-specific emergency procedures; jettison of fuel only authorized when necessary to prevent flight safety hazard; coordinate with ACA and JOC.

4. CSAR (Combat Search and Rescue)
4.1 CSAR Alert Posture. CSAR posture will be maintained at two levels:
  - ALERT I (Cover/Immediate Response): 1 HH-60G (Air Force) + 1 AH-64 (escort) within 30 minutes flying time from Primary Rescue Base (PRB) — PRB coordinates: 20.1500N 149.8500E (US Navy forward base). Active availability 24/7 MDIX.
  - ALERT II (Area Response): 2 USMC CH-53E or MV-22s at alternate recovery sites within 90 minutes flying time. Prepositioning by CH-53E/HC-130 crews near ROZ-01 during high-density strike operations.

4.2 Tasked Units.
  a. USAF CSAR: 38th Rescue Squadron (HH-60G/HC-130J) task-organized under the Theater Rescue Coordination Center (TRCC).
  b. USN/USMC: Carrier Air Wing Rescue and Marine Expeditionary Force (MEF) aviation detachments for maritime recoveries.
  c. Allied CSAR contributions: RAAF/ROK allied rescue assets integrated per LOA.

4.3 CSAR Frequencies and Comms.
  a. CSAR Primary Guard Net (UHF): 280.000 MHz AM — monitored by all air and maritime assets as CSAR guard.
  b. CSAR VHF Guard: 123.450 MHz FM (exercise non-IFR broadcast for SAR coordination).
  c. Rescue Coord Net (SATCOM Priority): INMARSAT-EXER-1 (Simulated: 2.5 kHz L-band) — for survivor data and long-haul coordination.
  d. Beacons and homing: ELT/PLB homing to 121.5/406 MHz will be included in SAR localization; receivers will be equipped with directional locators. All participants must enable encrypted survivability comms where available (e.g., PRC-163 with SATCOM patch).

4.4 CSAR Employment Procedures.
  a. Immediate Action: On pilot down, nearest aircraft will set CSAR guard channel to 280.000 MHz and report position/time to TRCC within 2 minutes. TRCC will push IR/SAR notifications to maritime forces and JOC.
  b. Rescue packages will use pre-approved ingress/egress lanes in ACO and will coordinate SEAD/escort with the suppression tasking authority.
  c. If airspace is denied/contested, CSAR will default to maritime-based recoveries (helicopter from surface combatants) and coordinate with maritime commander for maneuver.

5. SPACE SUPPORT
5.1 GPS Degradation / Spotty Service Warnings.
  a. Given the CONOPS and adversary EW/space-contest conditions, commanders must assume degraded and intermittent GPS navigation and timing during MDIX. The Space Support Element (SSE) and J5 will publish GPS Degradation Advisories on the Space Support Net (SSN) and via ACO not later than 30 minutes after detection.
  b. Adversary EW injection and localized GPS denial will be categorized:
     - Tier 1: Degraded GPS (loss of integrity/position jumps) — advisory.
     - Tier 2: Denied GPS (localized jamming over ROZ-02/ROZ-03) — limitation on GPS-reliant weapons; alternate nav required.
     - Tier 3: Spoofing suspected — immediate stand-down of autonomous weapons requiring positive nav confirm.
  c. Mitigation. Units must carry and be proficient in alternate navigation: INS, celestial, LORAN-like backup training, and map/compass coastal navigation for rotary wings. All GPS-dependent munitions require a validated contingency plan if Tier 2/3 is declared.

5.2 SATCOM Priorities and Management.
  a. SATCOM channels are a constrained resource; priorities reflect strategic tasking: (1) JFC/C2 and JOC, (2) ISR/OPIR data flow for COP, (3) CSAR and lifesaving comms, (4) logistics/sustainment messages, (5) exercise admin and media.
  b. SATCOM Allocation:
     - Primary SATCOM (UHF SATCOM) — exercise primary: UHF SATCOM NET A (dynamic assignment by SATCOM Cell). Use only for C2 and time-sensitive ISR push.
     - Secondary SATCOM (MIL-Ka/Ku LEO): Commercial Ka/Ku augmentation allowed under CAAs; all use must be routed through the Space Support Cell to authorize and schedule bandwidth. Forced denial or reallocation will be preannounced when possible.
  c. SATCOM Anti-Jam. Units with anti-jam SATCOM terminals (protected SATCOM waveforms, DAMA, and Link-16 SATCOM extension) will be prioritized for critical data feeds. Where available, Protected Tactical SATCOM (PTS) is the baseline for high-importance C2 links.

5.3 OPIR (Overhead Persistent Infrared) and SSA Data Feeds.
  a. OPIR and space-based ISR feeds are integrated into the Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2) COP. The Space Cell will disseminate OPIR cueing and SSA correlation via the Space Data Dissemination Net (SDDN).
  b. Data flow priority: Tactical warning (missile/ballistic threats), Maritime COP updates (surface track handover), and high-confidence ISR cueing for strike packages. Units must subscribe to the SDDN at mission pre-brief.
  c. Contested Space Contingency Procedures. If OPIR/space feeds are degraded, alternate cueing will be provided by airborne ISR (E-8, JSTARS-like), maritime deck sensors, and partner national assets per the ISR Collection Plan.

5.4 Spectrum & Space Emissions Control.
  a. All space-based transmissions and uplink commands must be coordinated through the Space Support Cell to avoid deconfliction and OPSEC breaches. Jamming or emissions used as red-team activity will be scheduled and promulgated in ACO.

6. COMMUNICATIONS
6.1 General Architecture. MDIX will employ a layered comms architecture emphasizing resilience: line-of-sight (LOS) VHF/UHF nets for tactical control, HF for long-haul redundancy, protected SATCOM for high-priority C2, and data-mesh/resilient tactical radio (e.g., Soldier/Battlefield radio waveforms) for ground/maritime distributed nodes. All comms use for exercise are unauthenticated/fictive where indicated unless pre-authorized.

6.2 Primary and Backup Frequency Nets (exercise allocations - not for release outside MDIX participants).
  a. JFC/JOC C2 Nets
     - Primary JOC SATCOM: PTS-EXER-01 (encrypted, assigned by Space Cell) — SatCOM channel pool (refer to Appendix COMMS-01)
     - Backup JOC HF: 8.136 MHz USB (HF long-haul JOC backup)
  b. Air Tasking and Control Nets
     - Air Tasking Net (ATN) Primary: UHF LOS 262.725 MHz AM (ATO sync and dynamic re-tasking)
     - ATN Backup: VHF Guard 136.625 MHz AM (local AOC to TACC)
     - Tactical Air Control Party (TACP) Ground-Air: VHF FM 30.780 MHz
  c. Air-to-Air
     - Tactical Air-to-Air: UHF FM 251.000 MHz (Link-16 gateway assigned per unit)
     - Link-16 Network: NET 1 — Crypto fill per component; JTIDS terminal scheduling via COMMO CELL.
  d. Maritime Nets
     - Primary Surface: HF 8414 kHz (USB) — secure long-haul maritime coordination
     - Ship-to-Ship Short-Range: VHF-FM 156.800 MHz (Channel 16) with exercise call-sign prefix "EX-"
  e. CSAR/Rescue
     - Primary CSAR Guard: UHF 280.000 MHz AM
     - CSAR Secondary: VHF 123.450 MHz FM
  f. EW/EMCON Control
     - EMCON Control Net (secure SATCOM): EMCON-CTRL-1 (broadcast enforced EMCON levels, jamming events, and authorized emissions)
     - EW Reporting Net (Unclassified): HF 5680 kHz USB.

6.3 Net Discipline and Call Signs.
  a. Net discipline is mandatory. Use brevity codes and standard phraseology per current US Joint Publications. Plain Language is preferred for multi-national interoperability unless crypto is pre-briefed.
  b. Exercise callsign conventions: Component prefix (e.g., "PACFLT-", "PACAF-") + mission type (e.g., "STRIKE", "TANKER", "CSAR") + numeric suffix. Example: PACAF-STRIKE-01, PACFLT-SHIP-05, JOC-CTRL-1.

6.4 EMCON and Anti-Jam Procedures.
  a. EMCON levels will be posted by the EMCON Authority and published in the ACO and COMMS Annex. Authorized EMCON deviations required for safety or mission-essential comms must be approved by the JOC.
  b. Anti-jam. Units will use frequency-hopping, spread-spectrum, and directional comms where available. Mesh and LPI/LPD waveforms will be preferred for distributed nodes. If jamming suspected, units will shift to pre-briefed alternate frequencies and report jamming source (bearing, strength) to the EW cell within 2 minutes.

6.5 COMSEC and OPSEC.
  a. All participants must follow COMSEC procedures; exercise-specific keying instructions are issued through the COMSEC account managers. Exercise comms designated UNCLASSIFIED simulation nets will still use discipline to avoid release of operationally sensitive data.
  b. OPSEC. Do not broadcast ship homeports, force numbers, or assured logistics schedules on unsecure nets. Use secure channels for logistics and force posture details.

1. GENERAL
1.1 Purpose. This Airspace Control Order (ACO) implements airspace control measures to support USINDOPACOM Multi-Domain Integration Exercise (MDIX) and associated contested logistics / degraded space readiness activities in the Western Pacific theater, 01–08 Mar 2026. It apportions, reserves, restricts, and coordinates airspace for joint and combined air, maritime, space-support, cyberspace, and information operations consistent with theater objectives DENY, DEGRADE, PROTECT, SUSTAIN, DESTROY as directed by the NDS Extract and NMS Theater Annex.
1.2 Authority. This ACO is published under authority of Commander, United States Indo-Pacific Command (CDRUSINDOPACOM) and executed by the Combined Air Operations Center (CAOC) at Andersen (Andersen CAOC callsign: PAC-CAOC), with Tactical Air Control Party (TACP), Maritime Airspace Coordination, and component airspace managers. All airspace users will comply with the controlling agencies and procedures listed herein.
1.3 Applicability. Applies to all US/Allied military aircraft, unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), contracted airlift, and participating civilian aircraft supporting MDIX. Non-exercise non-participating aircraft shall coordinate through appropriate diplomatic/overflight channels and obtain permission prior to entry.
1.4 Control Measures Summary. This ACO establishes Restricted Operating Zones (ROZs), Air Refueling Tracks (AR), Combat Air Patrol (CAP) stations, Transit Corridors (TC), and Kill Boxes (KB). All aircraft will carry current ATO/ATRS appendices, use designated frequencies, and comply with Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) code management and authentication procedures directed by PAC-CAOC.
1.5 Degraded Space/Communications Procedures. Anticipating degraded space-enabled services, CAOC implements a prioritized secure HF/UHF/VHF/tactical SATCOM fallback plan. Primary C2: UHF LOS (72.100–76.000 MHz Guard/selcal as per annex). Secondary: HF P2P net (6.209 MHz AM). SATCOM: Protected X-band (COMSEC required) only for authenticated net participants. EMCON restrictions in select ROZs (see ROZs) will limit emissions; scheduled periodic beacon bursts for identification will occur on 243.000 MHz discrete times listed in Table A (ATO Annex).
1.6 Authentication. Use three-part authentication: (1) callsign + mission code (per ATO), (2) two-word challenge-response from current authentication roster, (3) IFF mode/code verification. Failure to authenticate triggers immediate interception procedures or denial of airspace entry.
1.7 Coordination. All component airspace managers (PACAF A3, USFF Airspace, MARFORPAC, USARPAC aviation liaison) coordinate via the CAOC airspace cell. Real-time deconfliction provided by CAOC Airspace Battle Manager (ABM) on primary controlling frequency 282.000 MHz UHF (ABM callsign: PAC-ABM). Emergency diversion approvals via PAC-CAOC Commander (Andersen) or on-scene Tactical Director.

PHASE 1 (Days 1–3): Initial Strikes, SEAD, DCA Establishment

Key tasks:
- P1: Execute two daily suppression “windows” (W1 and W2) against simulated IADS/sensor/engagement clusters sufficient to open corridors for follow-on counterair and maritime effects. - P5: Establish continuous DCA presence with minimum two CAP orbits covering (a) primary air hub approach sector and (b) maritime LOC sector. CAP continuity is maintained by time-based handovers if datalink is degraded.
- P2: Begin counterair pressure and simulated strikes on air ops nodes to slow adversary response cycles.
- P3: Limited early maritime shaping—deny adversary reconnaissance-to-strike sequence rather than attempting full maritime neutralization.
- P4: Minimal initial non-kinetic shaping; prioritize collection and characterization to set conditions for Phase 2/3.

- P2: Daily rhythm of counterair pressure and simulated strikes against air generation nodes during windows that minimize blue exposure and maximize operational impact. Objective is measurable reduction in adversary sortie generation rates and ISR availability (exercise metrics).

- Launch emphasis: W2 execution, night CAP, RC-135 Sortie 4
- Planned fighter launches: 18–24 (lower density to accommodate resets and degraded comm procedures)

Daily CAP continuity requirement (P5):
- Maintain at least two CAP lines continuously (one hub defense, one maritime/LOC). Each CAP line requires 4–6 sorties per 24 hours depending on duration. MAAP funds this via P5 allocation and reserves.

5.3 Package Timing and Degraded Comms Control
- All major strikes/suppression missions are anchored to W1/W2 precision windows.
- If SATCOM/datalink drops, package lead executes pre-briefed timing gates:
  • Gate 1: push time (no earlier than planned)
  • Gate 2: abort time (if separation/deconfliction cannot be confirmed)
  • Gate 3: recovery stack time (procedural)
- Dynamic retasking is restricted to “retask windows” when AEHF connectivity is expected:
  • Retask Window R1: 0430Z–0500Z
  • Retask Window R2: 1630Z–1700Z
Outside R1/R2, only safety-of-flight and immediate threat warnings will be transmitted.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. ASSESSMENT CRITERIA (MEASURES OF EFFECTIVENESS)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assessment is effects-based and tied to each JIPTL priority. The AOC Strategy/Combat Assessment teams will compile daily metrics to inform the next ATO cycle.

PRIORITY 1 (P1) — A2/AD Node Cluster
MOE-P1.1 Corridor viability: Achieve and sustain at least two 90-minute “suppression windows” per day (Phase 1) and at least one 90-minute window per day (Phase 2–3) in which simulated IADS engagement probability is reduced to EXCON-defined threshold.
MOE-P1.2 Node suppression coverage: Suppress (simulated) at least 60% of prioritized IADS nodes in BE 0101–0110 during W1 on Days 1–2; maintain 40% on Days 3–7.
MOE-P1.3 Survivability: No simulated loss of HVAA attributable to unmitigated IADS corridors (tracked via EXCON adjudication).

PRIORITY 2 (P2) — Adversary Air & ISR Generation
MOE-P2.1 Sortie generation reduction: Demonstrate a sustained reduction in adversary simulated fighter sortie generation by 30% by end of Day 5 and 40% by end of Day 7 (relative to Day 1 baseline).
MOE-P2.2 Air tasking disruption: At least one daily period (minimum 2 hours) where adversary air C2 is assessed “degraded” (delayed tasking, reduced coordination) due to simulated effects.
MOE-P2.3 Blue counterair dominance: Blue achieves favorable simulated exchange ratio in air-to-air adjudication events during W1/W2 while maintaining CAP continuity.

PRIORITY 3 (P3) — Maritime Power Projection
MOE-P3.1 Maritime threat denial: Prevent adversary simulated surface action group from achieving weapon employment conditions against friendly logistics/capital units on 5 of 7 days (Days 2–8).
MOE-P3.2 Kill-chain disruption: On at least 4 days (Days 4–8), break the adversary maritime reconnaissance-to-strike sequence (cueing disrupted, targeting delayed, or engagement denied) as evidenced by ISR/cyber/EMS assessment.
MOE-P3.3 Joint integration: Execute at least one coordinated event per day where air sorties provide cueing/confirmation for simulated DDG/SSN fires (timed within 10 minutes of planned window).

PRIORITY 4 (P4) — Information/Networked Kill Chain
MOE-P4.1 Network degradation: By Day 7, demonstrate measurable adversary “sensor-to-shooter” latency increase (EXCON-defined) during at least one W1 or W2 window daily.
MOE-P4.2 Resilient C2: Successfully execute at least two mission packages (Days 6–8) with planned autonomy—no real-time updates required—while still meeting timing and deconfliction constraints.
MOE-P4.3 ISR characterization: Produce daily fused assessment of adversary network activity (from RC-135 and space ISR injects) with actionable recommendations for the next day’s allocation.

PRIORITY 5 (P5) — Friendly Protection & Sustainment
MOE-P5.1 CAP continuity: Maintain uninterrupted two-line CAP coverage for 90% of the exercise hours; any gaps must be risk-accepted by JFACC and mitigated procedurally.
MOE-P5.2 HVAA protection: Zero simulated losses of AWACS/tankers/RC-135 attributable to inadequate escort or CAP posture.
MOE-P5.3 Logistics corridor assurance: Demonstrate that air operations continue at planned sortie rates despite two or more contested logistics injects (fuel/munitions/maintenance constraints), with recovery to within 85% of planned capacity within 24 hours of each inject.

DAILY ASSESSMENT RHYTHM (to drive next ATO)
- +2 hours after W1: quick-look P1/P2 effects and corridor status for same-day adjustments (within limits).
- +2 hours after W2: preliminary daily MOE roll-up; identify refly needs and dynamic target nominations (exercise).
- End of day: MAAP/ATO update recommendations: shift up to ±10% sorties between priorities without revalidation, beyond that requires JFACC approval.

ENDSTATE (ATO Cycle 01)
By conclusion of Day 8, the force demonstrates the ability to (1) open and sustain operational corridors through an A2/AD environment, (2) reduce adversary air and maritime power projection, (3) degrade the adversary networked kill chain, and (4) protect friendly sustainment and HVAA—while operating under contested logistics and degraded space-enabled services with disciplined procedural control.

{
  "title": "National Defense Strategy (NDS) Extract — Western Pacific Integrated Deterrence and Multi-Domain Readiness (INDOPACOM)",
  "docType": "NDS",
  "authorityLevel": "SecDef",
  "content": "MEMORANDUM FOR: Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; Under Secretaries of Defense; Secretaries of the Military Departments; Commander, United States Indo-Pacific Command; Commanders of the Combatant Commands; Director, Joint Staff; Directors of Defense Agencies and Department of Defense Field Activities

FROM: Secretary of Defense

SUBJECT: National Defense Strategy (NDS) Extract — Western Pacific Integrated Deterrence and Multi-Domain Readiness (INDOPACOM) (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026)

DATE: 01 MAR 2026

CLASSIFICATION: UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO


1. PURPOSE.
   a. This memorandum provides a National Defense Strategy (NDS) extract to guide Department of Defense (DoD) prioritization, posture, and force development for the Western Pacific within the United States Indo-Pacific Command (USINDOPACOM) area of responsibility, with emphasis on integrated deterrence, campaigning, and enduring advantages under conditions of multi-domain contestation.
   b. This extract informs Joint Force planning, concept development, capability integration, and readiness activities supporting a time-bounded multi-domain integration exercise window of 01–08 March 2026. It is national-level guidance intended to shape downstream planning artifacts; it does not direct operational schemes of maneuver, tactical employment, or execution-level tasking.
   c. This extract highlights strategic considerations relevant to contemporary Joint Force employment in the Western Pacific: contested logistics and basing, degraded and intermittent space-enabled services, contested information environments, and rapid escalation dynamics involving a near-peer pacing threat. These conditions are treated as enduring features of the strategic environment rather than exercise-specific events.

2. STRATEGIC ENVIRONMENT (Parent Authority: 2022 NATIONAL DEFENSE STRATEGY OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA).
   a. This extract is derived from and implements the priorities and lines of effort articulated in the “2022 National Defense Strategy of the United States of America” (hereafter “2022 NDS”), including: (1) integrated deterrence; (2) campaigning; and (3) building enduring advantages. Where appropriate, this extract aligns to Joint doctrine for strategy-to-plans translation, including Joint Publication (JP) 5-0, Joint Planning; JP 3-0, Joint Campaigns and Operations; and supporting Joint doctrine for multi-domain integration and command and control.
   b. Pacing Threat. The People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the pacing challenge for the Department. The PRC is fielding and integrating a modern military designed to contest U.S. influence and presence in the Indo-Pacific, coerce U.S. allies and partners, and undermine the international rules-based order. The PRC’s anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) capabilities, long-range precision strike, undersea warfare investments, counterspace and cyber capabilities, and rapidly maturing intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) enterprise challenge U.S. freedom of maneuver across the air, maritime, space, and information domains. These capabilities are supported by a whole-of-state approach that leverages economic coercion, information operations, and gray-zone activities to achieve strategic aims below the threshold of armed conflict.
   c. Acute and Persistent Challenges. While the PRC remains the pacing threat, the Department will concurrently account for acute contingencies and destabilizing behaviors by other state and non-state actors, including malign cyber actors and proliferators, that can impose demands on global force management and enable opportunistic coercion. These challenges may create compounded risks by stretching logistics, readiness, and strategic attention. The Department will manage these risks through campaigning, posture resilience, and credible, flexible response options.
   d. Key Geography and Strategic Interests in the Western Pacific. The Western Pacific is central to U.S. national security and prosperity. U.S. strategic interests include: defense of the homeland and forward-deployed forces; honoring treaty commitments and ensuring the security of allies; maintaining open sea lines of communication (SLOCs) and freedom of navigation and overflight consistent with international law; preserving access to the global commons (maritime, air, space, and cyberspace); preventing coercive changes to the status quo (including attempts to resolve disputes by force); and sustaining a favorable balance of power that supports regional stability and economic vitality.
      (1) Key terrain includes the First and Second Island Chains, critical maritime chokepoints, and the sovereign territory and exclusive economic zones of allies and partners. The Department will respect sovereignty and operate consistent with international law while ensuring that coercion does not close or control the commons.
      (2) The Western Pacific’s dispersed geography, extended lines of communication, and dependency on air and maritime sustainment elevate the strategic importance of resilient logistics, diversified access, and protection of the defense industrial base and sealift/airlift capacity. Contested logistics is assessed as an enduring characteristic of high-end competition and potential conflict.
      (3) Space-enabled capabilities—positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT); satellite communications (SATCOM); missile warning; environmental monitoring; ISR; and data transport—are essential to Joint Force command and control (C2), long-range fires, integrated air and missile defense, and distributed operations. The Department anticipates intentional adversary actions to degrade, disrupt, or deny these services, resulting in intermittent coverage, localized gaps, or reduced fidelity. Resilience and graceful degradation are therefore strategic requirements, not technical preferences.
   e. Escalation Dynamics and the Information Environment. The PRC’s coercive actions may be calibrated for ambiguity and speed, leveraging information operations, cyber activity, and rapid faits accomplis designed to fracture allied cohesion and delay collective decision-making. The Department must be prepared to deter and, if necessary, respond to aggression under compressed timelines and contested information conditions, while preserving decision advantage consistent with U.S. values and law. Strategic messaging and credibility depend on demonstrable capability, readiness, and alliance unity.
   f. Implications for National Defense. The strategic environment demands that the Joint Force (1) sustain forward presence and campaigning activities that shape adversary choices; (2) ensure survivable, interoperable C2 across domains; (3) protect the force and critical infrastructure against precision strike and cyber attack; (4) expand logistics resilience and distributed sustainment; and (5) strengthen alliances and partnerships as a decisive strategic advantage. These imperatives align with the 2022 NDS emphasis on integrated deterrence and building enduring advantages.

3. STRATEGIC PRIORITIES (National-Level Effects and Doctrinal Justification).
   The Department will pursue the following strategic priorities in the Western Pacific. Each priority is expressed as a national-level effect and supported by Joint doctrine. These priorities are mutually reinforcing and must be integrated across policy, posture, force development, and campaigning.

   3.1. DENY PRC coercive objectives and military advantages in the Western Pacific by sustaining credible combat-credible forward posture, access, and freedom of maneuver across domains.
   a. Effect: DENY the pacing threat the ability to achieve a rapid fait accompli, present the United States and allies with a completed seizure or coercive outcome, or control key maritime/air approaches through A2/AD and intimidation.
   b. Justification: JP 3-0 emphasizes that Joint Force operations aim to gain and maintain freedom of action while denying adversaries their objectives. Denial underwrites deterrence by shaping adversary expectations of failure. JP 5-0 emphasizes aligning ends, ways, and means; denial is the required end to prevent coercive revision of the status quo.
   c. Strategic Implications: The Department will prioritize posture and access arrangements, resilient basing, and the ability to operate through contested domains. This includes strengthening interoperability and combined readiness with allies and partners to ensure that denial is multinational, not unilateral.

   3.2. DEGRADE adversary kill chains, ISR, and C2—especially counterspace, cyber, and long-range precision-strike enabling functions—through integrated deterrence, resilience, and multi-layered defense.
   a. Effect: DEGRADE the pacing threat’s ability to detect, track, target, and engage Joint and combined forces; reduce the effectiveness of coercive demonstrations and limited attacks; and impose uncertainty on adversary planning.
   b. Justification: JP 3-0 and JP 5-0 emphasize that degrading adversary capabilities and decision-making reduces risk and creates operational advantage. JP 3-30, Joint Air Operations, highlights the importance of achieving objectives through integrated planning that accounts for air, space, and information capabilities; degrading adversary integrated air defense systems (IADS), ISR, and C2 is central to reducing friendly vulnerability. The Department’s strategic requirement is resilience under attack, not perfect protection.
   c. Strategic Implications: The Department will emphasize survivability and redundancy in space-enabled services and C2, including the ability to operate with degraded SATCOM and intermittent space coverage. The Department will also strengthen cyber defense, mission assurance, and electromagnetic spectrum resilience to reduce the probability that adversary disruption produces strategic paralysis or fractures coalition cohesion.

   3.3. PROTECT U.S. treaty allies, partners, forward forces, and the global commons by reinforcing collective defense, integrated air and missile defense, and secure lines of communication.
   a. Effect: PROTECT allied sovereignty and U.S. forces; preserve freedom of navigation and overflight; and uphold international norms by ensuring that coercion cannot credibly threaten allied capitals, critical infrastructure, or the maritime/air commons.
   b. Justification: JP 3-0 frames protection as a core Joint function essential to maintaining freedom of action. JP 3-52, Joint Airspace Control, and JP 3-30 underscore the necessity of integrated air operations and airspace control in contested environments to reduce fratricide, protect high-value assets, and enable joint fires and maneuver. JP 5-0 reinforces that protection requirements must be incorporated early as constraints and risk considerations in campaign and contingency planning.
   c. Strategic Implications: The Department will deepen combined planning, information sharing, and interoperability to ensure protection is collective and credible. Protection includes defense of bases and ports, maritime approaches, critical undersea infrastructure, and the information environment that sustains public confidence and alliance cohesion.

   3.4. SUSTAIN a distributed Joint Force in the Western Pacific by strengthening contested logistics, industrial readiness, and the ability to fight through disruption.
   a. Effect: SUSTAIN Joint and combined forces under contested conditions by ensuring fuel, munitions, repair capacity, medical support, and lift are resilient, distributed, and rapidly reconstitutable; prevent strategic culmination caused by logistics interdiction or industrial shortfalls.
   b. Justification: JP 4-0, Joint Logistics, emphasizes that logistics is a foundational element of operational reach and endurance; in peer competition, logistics becomes a primary target. JP 3-0 highlights that sustaining the force is inseparable from maintaining initiative and tempo. JP 5-0 requires planners to integrate sustainment feasibility into the design of campaigns and contingency plans. Sustainment is therefore a strategic priority, not an enabling afterthought.
   c. Strategic Implications: The Department will prioritize stockpiles, prepositioning, diversified distribution networks, protected sealift/airlift, and agreements that enable access and support with allies and partners. The Department will also reinforce munitions production capacity, repair pipelines, and supply chain security to support extended operations and rapid replenishment.

   3.5. DESTROY adversary confidence in successful aggression by demonstrating the ability to impose unacceptable costs, including the credible defeat of aggression if deterrence fails.
   a. Effect: DESTROY the pacing threat’s confidence that it can initiate conflict on favorable terms, control escalation, or secure political objectives through limited force. This includes the capability and will to defeat aggression and restore the status quo ante consistent with U.S. interests and alliance commitments.
   b. Justification: JP 3-0 notes that credible combat power—paired with coherent objectives—underpins deterrence and compellence by shaping adversary decision-making. JP 5-0 emphasizes that strategy must be translated into executable plans that can achieve national objectives. While this memorandum does not direct operational execution, it affirms that the Department must maintain a credible defeat mechanism as the ultimate backstop to deterrence.
   c. Strategic Implications: The Department will maintain and communicate credible capabilities across domains, including long-range precision effects, undersea warfare, integrated air and missile defense, resilient C2, and combined joint force readiness. Demonstrations of capability will be aligned with strategic messaging to reinforce deterrence without unnecessary escalation.

4. COMMANDER’S INTENT (Secretary of Defense Intent).
   a. Purpose. Consistent with the 2022 NDS, the Department will strengthen integrated deterrence in the Western Pacific by synchronizing DoD activities with Allies and partners, interagency instruments, and—where appropriate—like-minded nations to prevent coercion and, if necessary, defeat aggression. The Department will campaign daily to shape the environment, reduce the risk of conflict, and ensure favorable conditions for U.S. decision-making.
   b. Method. The Department will:
      (1) Implement integrated deterrence by combining nuclear, conventional, cyber, space, and information capabilities with those of allies and partners, tailored to the pacing threat’s theory of victory and escalation calculus. This includes building combined readiness, interoperability, and shared understanding for collective action.
      (2) Campaign persistently to expose and counter coercion, build partner capacity, deepen access and posture resilience, and maintain credible forward presence without creating unnecessary escalatory pathways. The Department will prioritize activities that are sustainable, legally sound, and aligned with U.S. diplomatic objectives.
      (3) Build enduring advantages by accelerating capability integration, strengthening the defense industrial base, improving readiness generation, professional military education, talent management for highly technical missions, and strengthening mission assurance in contested space and cyber environments.
      (4) Institutionalize resilience as a strategic requirement: the Joint Force must be able to command, maneuver, and sustain operations under degraded communications, intermittent space support, contested electromagnetic spectrum, cyber disruption, and adversary long-range strike threats. The goal is continued effectiveness under attack, not dependency on uninterrupted connectivity.
      (5) Reinforce alliance cohesion as the center of gravity for U.S. strategy in the Indo-Pacific. Deterrence is strongest when the adversary assesses that aggression will be met with unified, capable, and timely collective response.
   c. Key Tasks (Strategic-Level). The Department directs the following strategic-level tasks to inform planning, programming, and prioritization; these are enduring tasks rather than execution orders:
      (1) Maintain credible deterrent posture in the Western Pacific consistent with U.S. treaty commitments and international law, including the ability to rapidly reinforce and operate through contested domains.
      (2) Strengthen combined planning and interoperability with allies and partners, including shared situational awareness and compatible C2 approaches, while protecting sensitive sources and methods.
      (3) Improve resilience and redundancy of space-enabled and terrestrial C2 and data transport to ensure continuity of command under attack. Planning assumptions must account for intermittent SATCOM and localized space service disruption.
      (4) Increase sustainment resilience and contested logistics readiness, to include diversified access, distributed stocks, and protected distribution. Plans and concepts will be assessed against logistics feasibility under adversary interdiction.
      (5) Align capability development and acquisition integration with Joint warfighting needs and validated requirements. Programmatic decisions will be informed by Joint concept-driven requirements and validated processes consistent with CJCSI 3170.01 (Joint Capabilities Integration and Development System) to ensure interoperable, coalition-relevant outcomes.
   d. Risk and Restraint. The Department will manage escalation risk by maintaining clear policy-aligned objectives, disciplined messaging, and adherence to the law of armed conflict. The Department will not cede strategic initiative; however, it will avoid actions that create unnecessary ambiguity regarding U.S. intent toward conflict initiation. Deterrence is strengthened by clarity of commitment, capability, and cohesion.

5. ENDSTATE.
   a. A secure, stable, and favorable balance of power in the Western Pacific in which:
      (1) The PRC is deterred from aggression and coercion; its leadership assesses that it cannot achieve strategic objectives through force or intimidation at acceptable cost or risk.
      (2) U.S. treaty allies and partners are assured, resilient, and increasingly interoperable, with strengthened collective capacity to defend sovereignty and uphold international law.
      (3) Freedom of navigation and overflight and the integrity of the global commons are preserved; SLOCs remain open and protected against coercive closure or control.
      (4) The Joint Force maintains credible, sustainable, and resilient forward posture and reinforcement capability, able to operate effectively despite degraded space-enabled services, contested electromagnetic spectrum, cyber disruption, and contested logistics.
      (5) DoD campaigning and enduring advantage initiatives measurably improve readiness, interoperability, and mission assurance, producing a Joint Force that can deter, and if required, defeat aggression while managing escalation and sustaining national will.

   b. This endstate reflects and operationalizes the 2022 NDS emphasis on integrated deterrence, campaigning, and building enduring advantages, translated for the Western Pacific strategic environment without prescribing operational-level execution.
