MEMORANDUM FOR: Commander, United States Indo-Pacific Command (CDRUSINDOPACOM)

FROM: Director, Plans and Policy (J5), United States Indo-Pacific Command

SUBJECT: Contingency Plan (CONPLAN) — Western Pacific Multi-Domain Integration Exercise (MDIX) / Contested Logistics and Degraded Space Readiness (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026)

DATE: 01 MAR 2026

REFERENCES:
a. Memorandum, CJCS to CDRUSINDOPACOM, “JSCP — INDOPACOM Western Pacific Multi-Domain Integration Exercise (MDIX) and Contested Logistics/Degraded Space Readiness,” 01 MAR 2026, UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO.
b. JP 5-0, Joint Planning.
c. JP 3-0, Joint Campaigns and Operations.
d. JP 3-52, Joint Airspace Control.
e. JP 3-30, Joint Air Operations.
f. JP 4-0, Joint Logistics.
g. JP 3-14, Space Operations.
h. JP 3-12, Cyberspace Operations.
i. JP 3-13, Information.
j. CJCSI 3170.01 (JCIDS), as applicable to capability gaps and urgent interoperability observations arising from MDIX.

1. PURPOSE. This CONPLAN translates JSCP tasking (Ref a) into an operational concept for a time-bound, notional multi-domain joint integration exercise in INDOPACOM’s Western Pacific area of responsibility, with baseline conditions of contested logistics, persistent EMS/cyber contestation, and degraded/intermittent space-enabled services. This plan is designed to drive realistic subordinate planning (including daily air tasking cycle inputs, joint collection management prioritization, and logistics synchronization) without providing tactical employment instructions or target-specific direction. This CONPLAN supports follow-on refinement into executable orders and supporting plans consistent with JP 5-0.

2. SITUATION.

   a. Strategic/Operational Context. From 01–08 MAR 2026, USINDOPACOM conducts MDIX to validate distributed posture, resilient C2, and sustainment under contested logistics and space coverage gaps. The adversary conducts calibrated coercion below armed conflict threshold, with rapid escalation options and a mature long-range precision strike complex. The operational problem is maintaining decision advantage and credible denial while preserving force survivability and sustainment when SATCOM/PNT/ISR transport are intermittent and logistics nodes are threatened (Refs a, c, g).

   b. Adversary Capabilities (Near-Peer, Pacific).
      (1) A2/AD Threat to Access and Sustainment. Adversary fields integrated air and maritime sensors and long-range strike systems that can threaten fixed and semi-fixed nodes (ports, airfields, fuel farms, communications sites), distribution routes, and high-demand platforms. Capability includes rapid targeting of signatures, pattern-of-life exploitation, and exploitation of predictable logistics rhythms.
      (2) Counterspace and Space-Enabled Denial. Adversary possesses capabilities to disrupt or degrade SATCOM, PNT, and ISR dissemination via jamming, spoofing, cyber effects on ground segments, and localized denial. Expected effects: intermittent loss of beyond-line-of-sight communications, timing errors, navigation inaccuracies, and degraded ISR transport.
      (3) Cyber/EMS Contestation. Adversary can conduct persistent cyber reconnaissance, intrusion attempts, and disruptive attacks against mission networks, logistics IT, and operational technology; employ electronic warfare to deny or degrade tactical data links, navigation aids, and radar/communications.
      (4) Information Operations (IO). Adversary conducts influence operations to undermine coalition cohesion, amplify incidents, and drive escalation narratives; attempts to create decision paralysis through ambiguity, misinformation, and attribution challenges (Ref i).

   c. Adversary Limitations/Vulnerabilities (Planning Assumptions).
      (1) Adversary kill chain effectiveness declines with dispersion, signature reduction, and deception; targeting confidence is sensitive to ISR continuity and data integrity.
      (2) Adversary must allocate finite ISR and strike resources across multiple domains and geographic approaches; overload and misdirection can impose operational dilemmas.
      (3) Adversary IO effectiveness is constrained by timely, credible allied messaging and operational transparency consistent with policy.

   d. Friendly Forces/Capabilities Available (Notional for Exercise Planning).
      (1) USINDOPACOM Joint Force Elements (categories):
          (a) Joint Force Air Component (JFACC) capabilities: multi-role fighter aviation; air mobility; airborne C2/relay; theater air and missile defense enablers; ISR platforms; aeromedical evacuation.
          (b) Joint Force Maritime Component (JFMCC) capabilities: surface combatants; undersea warfare elements as apportioned; maritime patrol; sealift coordination; mine countermeasure planning and limited execution injects.
          (c) Joint Force Land Component (JFLCC) / Army forces: theater sustainment, movement control, integrated air and missile defense contributions, expeditionary basing and airfield opening support, port opening elements, protection and security forces for nodes and convoys.
          (d) Marine forces: expeditionary advanced base operations (EABO) planning injects; littoral operations; aviation and ground logistics contributions; base defense.
          (e) Space/Cyber: USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM coordination and space mission assurance integration; USCYBERCOM coordination for defensive cyber operations (DCO), incident response, and hunt forward–style training injects; service cyber protection teams as available.
          (f) Special Operations (as applicable): liaison, ISR integration, and theater cooperation planning; no direct-action employment is directed by this CONPLAN.
      (2) Allies/Partners. Selected allies/partners participate in MDIX through liaison officers, information-sharing rehearsal, and limited combined events as directed by standing agreements and releasability rules. Combined integration focuses on C2 interoperability, maritime domain awareness, and logistics coordination under degraded communications.

   e. Theater Geography (Western Pacific).
      (1) Operating Environment. Maritime-dominant theater with extended lines of communication, constrained airfield/port capacity, and weather-driven operating impacts. Key terrain includes dispersed islands, chokepoints, and approaches through the First and Second Island Chains. Long distances impose fuel and maintenance demands; distributed operations require multiple nodes with varying infrastructure.
      (2) Implications. Geography favors an adversary’s long-range targeting of predictable hubs; friendly success depends on dispersion, mobility, deception, redundant distribution, and resilient C2 (Refs c, f). Airspace is complex with overlapping civil/military use; joint airspace control must function under intermittent data links (Ref d).

   f. Assumptions.
      (1) Contested logistics is continuous; distribution nodes may be disrupted with little warning (Ref f).
      (2) SATCOM availability is intermittent; PNT may be locally degraded; ISR transport may be delayed or denied (Ref g).
      (3) Cyber/EMS contestation is persistent, affecting both operational and sustainment systems (Refs h, i).
      (4) Exercise is conducted below threshold of armed conflict; rules of engagement and political constraints emphasize de-escalation and defensive posturing consistent with international law.
      (5) Host-nation support and access are variable and may require rapid adaptation to policy constraints.

   g. Constraints/Restraints.
      (1) Comply with applicable policy, standing rules for the use of force, and theater authorities; protect sensitive capabilities and tactics; adhere to releasability guidance.
      (2) Ensure safety and deconfliction with civil air/maritime traffic; implement risk controls consistent with joint and component safety programs.
      (3) No target-specific strike planning is directed within this CONPLAN; effects-based demonstrations will be simulated or executed within exercise control measures.

3. MISSION STATEMENT. USINDOPACOM conducts MDIX in the Western Pacific from 01–08 MAR 2026 to validate a theater-wide distributed posture and maneuver framework, resilient C2 under intermittent SATCOM/degraded PNT, integrated air-maritime-space-cyber operations, and contested logistics sustainment—demonstrating credible denial, degrading adversary kill-chain confidence through dispersion/deception, protecting the joint force and key nodes, and sustaining operational tempo with mission-type orders and rehearsed degraded-communications battle drills (Refs a–i).

4. CONCEPT OF OPERATIONS.

   a. Commander’s Intent.
      (1) Purpose: Prove the joint force can maintain decision advantage and credible deterrence in the Western Pacific while operating dispersed and sustaining forces when space-enabled services and logistics are contested.
      (2) Method: Employ distributed posture, resilient and redundant C2 pathways (PACE), mission-type orders, rapid reconstitution, deception/signature management, and prioritized sustainment distribution. Integrate air and maritime maneuver with space/cyber mission assurance and joint airspace control measures adaptable under degraded data links (Refs b–e, g–i).
      (3) End State (Exercise): Joint force demonstrates (a) ability to disperse and operate from multiple nodes with survivability and sustainment; (b) continued execution of prioritized tasks under communications loss; (c) effective joint airspace control and dynamic coordination despite degraded ISR/SATCOM; and (d) a logistics system that continues to deliver fuel, munitions, and critical parts under disruption with measured risk.

   b. Phasing (aligned to JP 3-0 construct; execution window 01–08 MAR 2026).

      PHASE 0 — SHAPE (pre-01 MAR preparation; validated during early exercise days)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Establish baseline distributed posture framework (primary/alternate operating locations, mobility triggers, EMCON guidance).
          (b) Confirm C2 architecture with PACE communications, data prioritization, and minimum essential information requirements.
          (c) Validate logistics posture for dispersion (prepositioning, load plans, movement control, alternate distribution methods).
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Issue mission-type orders emphasizing commander’s intent, delegated authorities, and “lost comms” battle drills (Ref b).
          (b) Establish joint airspace control plan adaptable under degraded data links (Ref d).
          (c) Conduct cyber hygiene surge and incident response rehearsals; establish cyber/EMS reporting and common operational picture (COP) degradation procedures (Refs h, i).
          (d) Coordinate space mission assurance measures: alternate PNT procedures, protected SATCOM prioritization, ISR dissemination workarounds (Ref g).

      PHASE 1 — DETER (01–02 MAR)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Demonstrate credible denial posture through dispersal readiness, defensive counterair/maritime defense integration (simulated or controlled execution).
          (b) Increase adversary uncertainty by reducing signatures, varying patterns, and employing deception injects.
          (c) Confirm coalition information-sharing and decision processes under communications constraints.
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Execute dispersal drill to selected distributed operating locations (DOLs) and maritime operating areas; validate command relationships and support agreements.
          (b) Practice defensive counterair and maritime coordination with joint airspace control measures; emphasize deconfliction with civil traffic and safety (Refs d, e).
          (c) Run “degraded SATCOM episode” injects to force transition to alternate C2 pathways and offline workflows.
          (d) Establish logistics distribution rhythm with variability; test movement control under route disruptions.

      PHASE 2 — SEIZE INITIATIVE (03–05 MAR)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Maintain operational tempo while space and cyber conditions deteriorate; demonstrate mission continuation with partial COP and delayed ISR.
          (b) Degrade adversary kill-chain confidence via dispersion, deception, and rapid reconstitution of disrupted nodes.
          (c) Validate cross-domain coordination among air, maritime, land, space, and cyber components with disciplined data prioritization.
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Conduct joint C2 resilience drills: transition between primary and alternate C2 nodes; practice “minimum essential information” reporting.
          (b) Execute integrated air-maritime events (simulated effects) requiring joint targeting coordination processes without reliance on continuous ISR feeds; validate time-sensitive coordination procedures at a conceptual level (Ref e).
          (c) Conduct logistics “shock” injects: loss of a primary node; fuel/munitions shortfall; cyber disruption to logistics IT; require re-routing, substitution, and prioritization (Ref f).
          (d) Exercise joint personnel recovery coordination (staff-level) under intermittent comms.

      PHASE 3 — DOMINATE (06–07 MAR)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Demonstrate ability to concentrate effects from dispersed positions while sustaining force protection and deconfliction.
          (b) Demonstrate theater sustainment endurance through redundancy and protected distribution.
          (c) Validate that joint airspace control and ATO/ACO processes remain viable with data link degradation and reduced SATCOM.
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Conduct a major joint integration event: combined air and maritime maneuver with space/cyber injects, emphasizing C2 discipline and safety (Refs c–e).
          (b) Execute reconstitution drills: repair/restoration of a degraded node, reallocation of sorties/maritime tasks, redistribution of sustainment.
          (c) Conduct information operations synchronization: proactive, truthful messaging; counter-misinformation drill; coalition narrative alignment (Ref i).

      PHASE 4 — STABILIZE (08 MAR and immediate post-exercise transition)
      (1) Objectives:
          (a) Transition to steady-state posture; capture lessons learned and capability gaps.
          (b) Produce prioritized observations for doctrine, training, materiel, leadership/education, personnel, facilities, and policy (DOTMLPF-P).
          (c) Identify JCIDS-relevant gaps and interoperability shortfalls for follow-on actions (Ref j).
      (2) Key Tasks:
          (a) Conduct hotwash and after-action reviews; compile assessment products and recommended changes to theater frameworks.
          (b) Update resilient C2 CONOPS, logistics playbooks, and joint airspace control procedures based on exercise results.
          (c) Issue follow-on planning guidance for supporting plans and capability submissions.

   c. Lines of Operation (LOO) (mutually supporting; assessed daily).

      LOO 1 — Distributed Posture & Maneuver (DENY)
      - Establish and sustain dispersed operating posture across air/maritime/land nodes; validate rapid dispersion and controlled concentration triggers; reduce predictability via variable patterns and EMCON.

      LOO 2 — Resilient Command and Control (DEGRADE/PROTECT)
      - Maintain effective decision-making with intermittent SATCOM and partial COP using PACE communications, mission-type orders, data prioritization, and offline workflows; validate cross-domain coordination and delegated authorities (Refs b, c, g).

      LOO 3 — Integrated Airspace Control & Air Operations (DENY/PROTECT)
      - Ensure safe, effective joint airspace control (ACO/ACP execution) under degraded data links; maintain deconfliction, ID procedures, and priority of air defense tasks (Refs d, e).

      LOO 4 — Contested Logistics & Sustainment (SUSTAIN/PROTECT)
      - Sustain operations with redundant distribution methods, dispersed stocks, rapid reroute, and protected movement control; maintain fuel, munitions, and critical parts delivery despite disruptions (Ref f).

      LOO 5 — Protection, Signature Management & Deception (PROTECT/DEGRADE)
      - Reduce vulnerability of nodes and platforms through integrated base defense, mobility, camouflage/concealment, emissions discipline, decoys (exercise-simulated), and rapid reconstitution planning.

      LOO 6 — Space/Cyber Mission Assurance & Information Resilience (DEGRADE)
      - Integrate space mission assurance measures; execute defensive cyber operations and incident response; sustain trusted information flows and counter adversary misinformation (Refs g–i).

   d. Decisive Points (exercise-defined conditions that determine success of the operational approach).
      (1) DP1: Joint force successfully transitions from steady-state communications to alternate C2 (PACE) within defined time standards while maintaining safe airspace control and mission continuity (Refs b, d).
      (2) DP2: Sustained sortie/maritime task generation continues after loss or degradation of a primary logistics node through redistribution and prioritization without unsafe degradation of operations (Ref f).
      (3) DP3: Joint airspace control remains effective during data link degradation (fallback ID procedures, altitude blocks, procedural control) while maintaining civil deconfliction (Ref d).
      (4) DP4: Coalition information-sharing continues under releasability constraints and comms degradation using preplanned products, release procedures, and liaison networks.
      (5) DP5: Cyber incident response contains and restores mission-essential functions within acceptable time, with validated manual/alternate processes for logistics and C2 (Ref h).
      (6) DP6: Space degradation injects (PNT/SATCOM/ISR transport) do not halt decision cycles; alternate nav/timing and reporting procedures are executed effectively (Ref g).

5. ADVERSARY COURSES OF ACTION (COA) (notional for exercise inject design).

   COA 1 — “Gray-Zone Pressure with Precision ISR”
   - Adversary uses maritime and air presence, IO narratives, and cyber probing to create ambiguity; applies localized jamming and intermittent SATCOM disruption to stress C2; conducts aggressive ISR to map dispersed nodes and logistics patterns. Intended effect: deter friendly maneuver, force consolidation, and induce political friction.

   COA 2 — “Kill-Chain Acceleration Against Logistics”
   - Adversary prioritizes disruption of sustainment: cyber effects on logistics IT, EW against navigation/port operations, and simulated long-range strike threats against predictable hubs. Intended effect: create fuel/munitions shortfalls, slow operational tempo, and compel risk acceptance or withdrawal.

   COA 3 — “Space-Enabled C2 Disruption with IO Amplification”
   - Adversary degrades SATCOM and PNT locally while amplifying misinformation regarding incidents and alleged escalation. Intended effect: fragment coalition decision-making, slow authorization cycles, and undermine confidence in data integrity.

6. FRIENDLY COURSES OF ACTION (RECOMMENDED COA).

   COA R — “Distributed Resilience with Controlled Concentration”
   a. Summary. Employ a dispersed posture with mission-type orders and robust PACE communications; prioritize sustainment dispersion and protected distribution; operate joint airspace control with procedural fallbacks; integrate space/cyber mission assurance; and selectively concentrate effects (simulated/demonstrative) when decisive points require, then rapidly re-disperse to reduce targetability.

   b. Why COA R. This approach directly implements JSCP priorities (DENY/DEGRADE/PROTECT/SUSTAIN) under baseline degraded space and contested logistics, while minimizing single-point dependencies and enabling continued operations with partial information (Refs a–i).

   c. Risk and Mitigation.
      (1) Risk: Reduced efficiency due to dispersion and procedural airspace control. Mitigation: preplanned airspace control measures, rehearsed battle drills, and minimum essential coordination procedures (Refs d, e).
      (2) Risk: Logistics shortfalls from disrupted distribution. Mitigation: prepositioned stocks, alternate distribution, prioritized consumption controls, and movement control redundancy (Ref f).
      (3) Risk: COP degradation increases fratricide/safety hazard. Mitigation: strict ID and procedural control measures, clear ROE/standing guidance, and conservative deconfliction (Ref d).
      (4) Risk: Cyber compromise of sustainment/C2 systems. Mitigation: DCO posture, segmentation, manual fallback processes, and incident response rehearsals (Ref h).

7. FORCE REQUIREMENTS (general categories; refined in OPLAN/EXORD and component supporting plans). The following categories are required to execute COA R and achieve decisive points. Quantities and sourcing are determined by force allocation processes and exercise control.

   a. Air Component (JFACC).
      (1) Multi-role tactical aviation (defensive counterair emphasis; integration with maritime operations).
      (2) Airborne C2/relay and battle management (with line-of-sight and gateway options).
      (3) Air mobility: intra-theater lift, aerial refueling, aeromedical evacuation.
      (4) ISR collection platforms and dissemination nodes (with degraded dissemination workarounds).
      (5) Theater air and missile defense enablers (integrated with joint airspace control and base defense).

   b. Maritime Component (JFMCC).
      (1) Surface combatants for presence, air defense, and maritime security coordination.
      (2) Maritime patrol and reconnaissance for domain awareness and cueing.
      (3) Logistics support coordination (replenishment planning, distribution deconfliction).
      (4) Mine warfare planning support (limited injects to stress routing and port access assumptions).

   c. Land Component / Army (JFLCC / USARPAC).
      (1) Theater sustainment command functions: distribution management, contracting coordination, movement control, and sustainment COP.
      (2) Expeditionary airfield/port opening capabilities (planning and limited execution injects).
      (3) Integrated air and missile defense contributions and base defense enablers.
      (4) Engineering support for rapid repair and reconstitution of austere nodes.

   d. Marine Forces (MARFORPAC).
      (1) Expeditionary basing and littoral logistics planning cells; node security and sustainment detachments as available.
      (2) Aviation support for distributed operations (as apportioned).
      (3) Deception/signature management support (exercise-controlled).

   e. Space/Cyber/Information.
      (1) Space mission assurance coordination team; alternate PNT and SATCOM prioritization procedures (Ref g).
      (2) Cyber protection teams / DCO coordination elements; incident response liaison with USCYBERCOM (Ref h).
      (3) Information operations coordination cell to synchronize messaging and counter misinformation (Ref i).

   f. Joint Enablers.
      (1) Joint communications support with deployable packages for austere nodes.
      (2) Medical support and patient movement coordination under degraded comms.
      (3) Security cooperation and liaison networks for access, HNS, and combined interoperability.

   g. Force Allocation Priority Table (notional; to inform sourcing and ATO/ACO planning).

      TABLE 1 — FORCE ALLOCATION PRIORITIES (MDIX 01–08 MAR 2026)
      +------------------------------+------------------------------+----------+------------------------------+------------------------------+
      | Capability Category          | Primary Purpose              | Priority | Key Dependencies              | Exercise Validation Focus     |
      +------------------------------+------------------------------+----------+------------------------------+------------------------------+
      | Airborne C2/Relay            | Resilient C2 / battle mgmt   | 1        | Spectrum access; LOS nets     | PACE transition; COP loss     |
      | Air Mobility / Refuel        | Sustain distributed ops      | 1        | Airspace control; fuel stocks | Disrupted node resupply       |
      | Base Defense / Security      | Protect nodes & dispersal    | 1        | Early warning; comms          | Rapid reposition; ID drills   |
      | Movement Control / JLOTS*    | Contested distribution       | 1        | Port/airfield access          | Reroute under disruption      |
      | Multi-role Tactical Aviation | Denial demonstration         | 2        | ACO/ACO updates; ID measures  | Procedural control operations |
      | Surface Combatants           | Maritime defense / presence  | 2        | Maritime domain awareness     | C2 under comm degradation     |
      | ISR Collection               | Awareness / cueing           | 2        | Dissemination pathways        | Delayed ISR workflow          |
      | Engineering / Rapid Repair   | Reconstitution               | 3        | Parts/tools; security         | Restore node functionality    |
      | Cyber Protection / IR        | Preserve mission systems     | 1        | Authorities; forensic support | Restore MEFs under attack     |
      | Space Mission Assurance      | PNT/SATCOM resilience        | 1        | USSPACECOM coordination       | Alt PNT; SATCOM prioritization|
      | IO / Public Affairs sync     | Narrative resilience         | 2        | Releasability; liaison        | Counter-misinformation drill  |
      +------------------------------+------------------------------+----------+------------------------------+------------------------------+
      *JLOTS referenced conceptually; execution per authorities and exercise design.

8. LOGISTICS CONCEPT (JP 4-0 aligned; designed for contested logistics conditions).

   a. Logistics Intent. Sustain distributed joint operations during MDIX by designing logistics to be survivable, redundant, and adaptable: disperse stocks; vary distribution patterns; prioritize mission-essential requirements; and enable rapid reroute and reconstitution when nodes are degraded or denied.

   b. Logistics Concept of Support.
      (1) Distribution.
          (a) Employ a hub-and-spoke concept with multiple alternates rather than a single primary hub. Maintain the ability to shift between air, surface, and prepositioned/forward stocks based on threat and access.
          (b) Implement movement control with redundant routing options and preplanned “route denial” responses (alternate ports/airfields, transload points, and staging areas not identified in this CONPLAN).
          (c) Synchronize distribution with EMCON and deception guidance to reduce predictability.
      (2) Supply (Classes I, III, V, VIII, IX priority).
          (a) Class III (Fuel): Establish dispersed fuel posture; prioritize aviation and critical maritime/ground requirements; enforce consumption discipline during disruption injects.
          (b) Class V (Munitions): Exercise controlled allocation and simulated expenditure reporting; validate secure storage, accountability, and rapid redistribution procedures.
          (c) Class IX (Repair Parts): Prioritize mission-critical parts; test alternate sourcing and cannibalization policy decision points (exercise-simulated approvals).
          (d) Class VIII (Medical): Validate distributed medical logistics, cold chain resilience, and patient movement coordination under comm degradation.
      (3) Maintenance.
          (a) Use distributed maintenance planning; employ mobile support teams as available; practice maintenance data reporting with offline capture and delayed sync.
          (b) Validate ability to continue safe operations with partial maintenance IT outages using manual procedures.
      (4) Contracting and Host-Nation Support.
          (a) Coordinate contracting to reduce single-point vendor dependencies; incorporate payment/communication disruptions in injects.
          (b) Validate HNS request and coordination processes under releasability and comm constraints.
      (5) Protection of Sustainment.
          (a) Integrate base defense for logistics nodes; coordinate with airspace control for local defense activities and restricted operating zones (Ref d).
          (b) Implement cyber protections for logistics IT; test manual fallback (paper/standalone) for critical movements and inventory.

   c. Logistics Synchronization and Battle Rhythm.
      (1) Establish a Joint Logistics Coordination Board (JLCB) cadence aligned with ATO/ACO cycles (Ref e) to prioritize lift, fuel, and critical supplies.
      (2) Maintain a Logistics Common Operational Picture (LOGCOP) with “degraded mode” procedures (minimum essential fields, delayed reporting tolerances, and alternate reporting channels).
      (3) Define “Sustainment Priorities of Support” by phase (Table 2).

      TABLE 2 — SUSTAINMENT PRIORITIES OF SUPPORT BY PHASE (NOTIONAL)
      +---------+------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
      | Phase   | Priority of Support          | Primary Logistics Emphasis                   |
      +---------+------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+
      | 0 Shape | C2 nodes, node opening       | Preposition; comm packages; repair stocks    |
      | 1 Deter | Dispersed air/mar nodes       | Fuel distribution; mobility spares; security |
      | 2 Seize | Endurance under disruption   | Reroute; substitution; rapid reconstitution  |
      | 3 Dom   | Controlled concentration      | Surge lift/refuel; maintenance throughput    |
      | 4 Stab  | Reset and lessons learned     | Reconstitution; accountability; retrofit     |
      +---------+------------------------------+---------------------------------------------+

9. COMMAND AND CONTROL (C2) (JP 3-0, JP 5-0 aligned; resilient under degraded space).

   a. Command Relationships (notional; per existing authorities and exercise directives).
      (1) CDRUSINDOPACOM serves as supported commander for MDIX overall integration.
      (2) Component commanders (JFMCC, JFACC, JFLCC, MARFORPAC) execute assigned tasks and provide forces/capabilities per allocation; coordinate through joint boards, centers, and working groups.
      (3) Space and cyber coordination occurs through established support relationships: USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM integrates space mission assurance; USCYBERCOM coordination for DCO/IR alignment and deconfliction (Refs g, h).

   b. C2 Architecture and PACE Communications.
      (1) Primary: SATCOM-enabled joint networks and standard operational COP services (acknowledged intermittent).
      (2) Alternate: Line-of-sight networks, terrestrial relays, and airborne gateways; procedural reporting formats for ATO/ACO essential coordination.
      (3) Contingency: Low-bandwidth data paths, store-and-forward messaging, scheduled windows, and courier-assisted transfer where feasible.
      (4) Emergency: Prebriefed lost-communications plans; commander’s intent execution; time-based and event-based decision triggers; safety-of-flight and airspace control procedural measures (Refs b, d).

   c. Decision-Making and Mission Command.
      (1) Implement mission-type orders emphasizing outcomes, constraints, authorities, and triggers for dispersion/concentration (Ref b).
      (2) Establish “Minimum Essential Information Requirements” to avoid overloading degraded networks: force protection, airspace control changes, sustainment status, and time-critical safety information.
      (3) Delegate decision authorities where appropriate for safety and continuity (e.g., airspace procedural control activation, logistics reroute execution), consistent with policy and commander’s intent.

   d. Joint Boards/Cells and Integration.
      (1) Joint Air Operations Center (JAOC) functions (Ref e): maintain ATO cycle with degraded operations procedures (manual backups, reduced product set, prioritized dissemination).
      (2) Airspace Control Authority (ACA) execution (Ref d): ensure ACO/ACP updates are disseminated through PACE; define procedural airspace control packages when digital dissemination fails.
      (3) Joint Fires / Effects Coordination: exercise staff-level coordination for integrated effects without target-specific planning; focus on process resilience and deconfliction.
      (4) Space/Cyber/IO Integration Cell: synchronize space mission assurance, cyber defense posture, and information activities; coordinate with coalition liaison elements for timely, releasable updates.

   e. Reporting and Assessment.
      (1) Measures of Performance (MOP): PACE transitions executed; ACO/ATO dissemination timelines; logistics delivery timeliness under disruption; cyber incident containment/restoration times; node reconstitution timelines.
      (2) Measures of Effectiveness (MOE): ability to maintain operational tempo; reduced operational predictability; sustained safety and deconfliction; continued coalition coordination under degraded comms; demonstrated endurance of sustainment.
      (3) After-Action Products: consolidated observations, gap analysis, recommended updates to theater frameworks; JCIDS-relevant capability gap nominations and interoperability issues (Ref j).

10. COORDINATING INSTRUCTIONS.
   a. Exercise Control. All events are subject to exercise control measures, safety constraints, and policy limitations. Effects requiring simulated actions will be executed through approved exercise constructs.
   b. Information Security/Releasability. Maintain strict data handling, classification, and releasability discipline. Use preapproved release packages and liaison channels for coalition sharing.
   c. Deconfliction. Ensure maritime and airspace deconfliction with civil traffic and partner operations; employ procedural controls when required (Ref d).
   d. Safety. Prioritize safety-of-flight and navigation under degraded PNT; implement conservative procedural measures when uncertainty increases.

11. ADMINISTRATION AND LOGISTICS (PLAN MAINTENANCE).
   a. Plan Status. This CONPLAN is effective for MDIX planning and execution window 01–08 MAR 2026 and will be updated upon completion based on lessons learned.
   b. Supporting Plans/Annexes (to be developed/refined by components and directorates).
      (1) Resilient C2 CONOPS (PACE, data prioritization, degraded COP procedures).
      (2) Contested Logistics Support Plan (distribution, node reconstitution, contracting continuity).
      (3) Joint Airspace Control Degraded Operations Procedures (procedural control packages).
      (4) Cyber Incident Response Playbook for mission and sustainment systems.
      (5) Space Mission Assurance Integration Guide (alternate PNT, SATCOM prioritization, ISR dissemination workarounds).

12. SUMMARY. This CONPLAN operationalizes JSCP tasking by focusing MDIX on distributed posture, resilient C2, contested logistics endurance, and space/cyber mission assurance. Success is defined by the joint force’s ability to continue safe, effective operations and sustainment under intermittent SATCOM, degraded PNT, and persistent cyber/EMS contestation—while demonstrating credible denial and coalition integration consistent with JP 5-0, JP 3-0, JP 3-52, and related doctrine.

FROM: Director, Plans and Policy (J5), United States Indo-Pacific Command

SUBJECT: OPERATIONS PLAN (OPLAN) — Western Pacific Multi-Domain Integration Exercise (MDIX) / Contested Logistics and Degraded Space Readiness (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026)

REFERENCES:
a. Memorandum, CJCS to CDRUSINDOPACOM, “JSCP — INDOPACOM Western Pacific Multi-Domain Integration Exercise (MDIX) and Contested Logistics/Degraded Space Readiness,” 01 MAR 2026, UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO.

1. (U//FOUO) SITUATION.

   a. (U//FOUO) General. This OPLAN refines the cited CONPLAN into an executable, exercise-focused order framework for MDIX conducted 01–08 MAR 2026 in the Western Pacific area of responsibility. MDIX is a below-armed-conflict, joint/combined integration exercise intended to validate distributed posture, mission command under degraded communications, and sustainment under contested logistics while integrating air, maritime, space, cyber, and information disciplines in a dynamic, safety-controlled environment. This OPLAN provides operational-level direction consistent with JP 5-0 and JP 3-0. It deliberately avoids target-specific strike direction and omits any tactical-level employment details that are not required for joint synchronization.

   b. (U//FOUO) Operational Environment.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Geography and Distance. The Western Pacific theater is maritime-dominant with extended lines of communication (LOCs), a limited number of high-capacity ports and airfields, and significant weather variability. Joint force success depends on dispersion, mobility, deception, redundant distribution, and resilient command and control (C2). Long-range mobility and sustainment demands (fuel, maintenance, munitions, medical) are decisive constraints (JP 4-0).
      (2) (U//FOUO) Civil Considerations. Airspace and sea lanes include dense civil traffic requiring disciplined joint airspace control measures and maritime deconfliction, particularly during communications degradation. Host-nation and access permissions vary by location and are subject to exercise control (EXCON) policy injects.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Space/Cyber/EMS Conditions. Exercise conditions include intermittent SATCOM availability, localized PNT degradation, variable ISR transport latency, and persistent cyber/EMS contestation affecting both operational and sustainment systems (JP 3-14, JP 3-12). These conditions will be introduced via controlled injects, with safety-of-flight protections and pre-coordinated risk controls.

   c. (U//FOUO) Adversary (Near-Peer State, Pacific). A near-peer state adversary (OPFOR) conducts calibrated coercion below the armed conflict threshold, with rapid escalation options. OPFOR employs an integrated long-range precision strike complex supported by multi-domain ISR and influence activities.
      (1) (U//FOUO) A2/AD Threat to Access and Sustainment. OPFOR can threaten fixed and semi-fixed nodes (ports, airfields, fuel storage, communications sites) and distribution routes, exploiting predictable logistics rhythms, signatures, and pattern-of-life.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Counterspace and Space-Enabled Denial. OPFOR can disrupt SATCOM and degrade PNT and ISR dissemination through jamming/spoofing and cyber effects against ground/transport segments, producing intermittent BLOS loss, timing errors, and navigation inaccuracies.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Cyber/EMS Contestation. OPFOR conducts persistent cyber reconnaissance and disruptive attempts against mission networks, logistics IT (including movement and inventory management), and operational technology; simultaneously contests tactical data links and navigation aids.
      (4) (U//FOUO) Information Operations. OPFOR seeks to undermine coalition cohesion and induce decision paralysis through misinformation, narrative framing, and attribution ambiguity.

   d. (U//FOUO) Friendly Forces.
      (1) (U//FOUO) USINDOPACOM. USINDOPACOM forms a Joint Task Force (JTF-MDIX) for exercise execution, with functional components designated JFACC, JFMCC, JFLCC, and JFSOCC (liaison-focused), and coordination with USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM and cyber protection elements. Component capabilities include multi-role tactical aviation, air mobility, airborne C2/relay, maritime surface and undersea forces, expeditionary basing elements, air and missile defense enablers, theater sustainment, and defensive cyber operations.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Allies/Partners. Selected allies/partners participate through liaison officers, limited combined events, maritime domain awareness integration, and logistics coordination subject to releasability constraints. Combined integration will emphasize interoperability under communications degradation and shared situational awareness (SA) using pre-agreed data standards and manual/voice fallback procedures.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Interagency. Coordination with U.S. Government partners occurs as required for information activities, space/cyber incident reporting pathways, and safety/host-nation considerations.

   e. (U//FOUO) Assumptions.
      (1) Contested logistics and periodic disruption of distribution nodes are continuous conditions.
      (2) SATCOM is intermittent; PNT is locally degraded; ISR transport is delayed/denied episodically.
      (3) Cyber/EMS contestation persistently affects operational and sustainment systems.
      (4) Exercise remains below armed conflict threshold; political constraints emphasize de-escalation and defensive posturing consistent with international law and standing rules for the use of force.
      (5) Access, basing, and overflight permissions may change with minimal notice under EXCON injects.

   f. (U//FOUO) Constraints/Restraints.
      (1) Comply with applicable policy, standing rules for use of force (SRUF), and theater authorities.
      (2) Protect sensitive capabilities/tactics; adhere to releasability guidance and operational security (OPSEC).
      (3) Ensure safety and deconfliction with civil air/maritime traffic; implement risk controls per component safety programs.
      (4) No target-specific strike planning or real-world target nomination is authorized in this OPLAN. Any kinetic effects are simulated or executed solely within EXCON-approved training constraints.

2. (U//FOUO) MISSION.

USINDOPACOM conducts MDIX in the Western Pacific from 01–08 MAR 2026 to validate theater-wide distributed posture and maneuver, resilient C2 under intermittent SATCOM and degraded PNT, integrated air–maritime–space–cyber operations, and contested logistics sustainment—demonstrating credible denial, degrading adversary kill-chain confidence through dispersion/deception, protecting the joint force and key nodes, and sustaining operational tempo with mission-type orders and rehearsed degraded-communications battle drills.

3. (U//FOUO) EXECUTION.

   a. (U//FOUO) Commander’s Intent.
      (1) Purpose. Demonstrate that a joint/combined force can maintain decision advantage and credible deterrence while operating dispersed and sustaining forces when space-enabled services are intermittent and logistics nodes are threatened.
      (2) Method. Employ distributed posture; mission command with mission-type orders; resilient and redundant C2 (PACE); disciplined emissions control, signature management, and deception; and prioritized, risk-informed sustainment distribution. Integrate joint airspace control measures adaptable under degraded data links; synchronize maritime maneuver and air operations with space/cyber mission assurance and information activities to maintain initiative and reduce OPFOR targeting confidence.
      (3) End State. Joint force demonstrates: (a) distributed operations across multiple nodes with survivability and sustainment; (b) continued execution of prioritized tasks during comms loss; (c) effective joint airspace control and dynamic coordination despite degraded ISR/SATCOM; (d) logistics resilience delivering fuel, munitions, and critical parts under disruption; and (e) validated observations informing interoperability/capability gaps for follow-on reporting consistent with CJCSI 3170.01.

   b. (U//FOUO) Concept of Operations / Scheme of Maneuver.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Operational Approach. JTF-MDIX conducts an eight-day, phased exercise that stresses the joint force across: (a) distributed basing and maneuver; (b) degraded space services; (c) contested cyber/EMS; and (d) logistics disruption with time-sensitive reconstitution and reroute drills. The “maneuver” construct is operational and non-kinetic in nature: it is expressed as posture changes, maritime/air presence shifts, expeditionary node activation, and C2 adaptation rather than target engagement.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Phasing (JP 3-0). The phases below align to the execution window and are synchronized through daily Joint Synchronization Meetings (JSM), the air tasking cycle (JP 3-30), and logistics synchronization boards (JP 4-0).

         (a) PHASE 0 — SHAPE / POSTURE VALIDATION (D0–D1; 01–02 MAR).
             1. Objectives: establish baseline distributed posture; confirm access/status of designated main operating bases (MOBs), forward operating sites (FOS), and cooperative locations (CLs) authorized by EXCON; validate joint airspace control procedures (JP 3-52); establish PACE communications; initiate cyber defense posture and space mission assurance procedures.
             2. Key Tasks: communications rehearsals (SATCOM loss drills); manual ATO/ACO dissemination fallback procedures; logistics node readiness checks; deception/signature baseline establishment; allied liaison integration and releasability rehearsals.

         (b) PHASE I — DETER / INITIATIVE UNDER CONTESTATION (D2–D3; 03–04 MAR).
             1. Objectives: demonstrate credible denial posture through distributed air and maritime presence; begin contested logistics operations with reroute/alternate sourcing; validate degraded PNT tactics/procedures at the operational level (navigation risk management, timing discipline); integrate maritime domain awareness with air operations despite ISR transport delays.
             2. Key Tasks: surge readiness and sortie generation from dispersed nodes; maritime screening and escort training injects; expeditionary node activation (airfield/port opening elements) and base defense rehearsals; information activities to counter OPFOR narratives.

         (c) PHASE II — SEIZE DECISION ADVANTAGE / RESILIENT C2 (D4–D6; 05–07 MAR).
             1. Objectives: operate through multiple comms outages and cyber incidents while maintaining commander’s priorities; execute joint dynamic retasking processes with degraded SA; stress joint logistics with simulated node disruption and contested LOCs; demonstrate reconstitution and rapid relocation for selected capabilities.
             2. Key Tasks: implement mission-type orders with pre-planned decision points; exercise alternate C2 nodes; execute joint personnel recovery (PR) coordination drills (simulated) under degraded comms; conduct joint airspace control transitions (procedural control emphasis) when data links are degraded.

         (d) PHASE III — TRANSITION / AFTER ACTION CONSOLIDATION (D7; 08 MAR).
             1. Objectives: consolidate dispersed posture; account for personnel/equipment; restore networks and logistics systems; capture lessons, interoperability gaps, and capability shortfalls for CJCSI 3170.01-aligned reporting; execute combined hotwash.
             2. Key Tasks: redeployment planning; maintenance recovery; munitions/fuel reconciliation; cybersecurity incident closure and reporting; finalize exercise observations.

      (3) (U//FOUO) Joint Air Scheme (JP 3-30; JP 3-52).
         (a) JFACC establishes an Air Operations Center (AOC) core with distributed/alternate mission teams to function during comms degradation. The ATO cycle will use digital dissemination when available and pre-briefed execution matrices (mission-type orders) when not.
         (b) Airspace Control: The Airspace Control Plan (ACP) and Airspace Control Order (ACO) will emphasize simple, deconflicted procedural control options as primary during degraded data links, with positive control retained where feasible. Pre-coordinated transit corridors, altitude blocks, and timing windows will be used to reduce reliance on dynamic reroutes during comms outages, while maintaining safety and civil deconfliction.
         (c) Prioritized Air Missions (exercise objectives): defensive counterair (DCA) and integrated air and missile defense (IAMD) support (simulated); airborne C2/relay; ISR and maritime domain awareness support; air mobility for distributed sustainment; aeromedical evacuation drills; and limited OCA-like simulated effects within training constraints (no real-world target nomination).

      (4) (U//FOUO) Maritime Scheme.
         (a) JFMCC conducts distributed maritime presence operations in designated exercise sea areas to complicate OPFOR ISR, protect sea LOC training lanes, and enable maritime domain awareness integration with the JFACC/JFLCC. Surface forces train in escort, screening, and emissions-controlled maneuver; undersea forces (as allocated) provide simulated ISR and sea denial effects within exercise control.
         (b) Mine countermeasure planning is exercised through staff planning injects and limited at-sea events as available; no real-world hazard to navigation will be created.
         (c) Maritime logistics and sustainment training focuses on replenishment planning, alternate port selection (as authorized), and expeditionary offload concepts consistent with JP 4-0.

      (5) (U//FOUO) Land / Expeditionary Basing Scheme.
         (a) JFLCC and Marine forces activate and sustain expeditionary nodes (airfield/port opening, refuel/rearm points, distributive supply points) to enable dispersed air and maritime operations. Base defense, convoy/route security training injects, and CBRN readiness checks (as directed) will be conducted.
         (b) IAMD contributions (where assigned) integrate with joint air defense planning and reporting, focusing on sensor-to-shooter information pathways and procedural backups under comms degradation.

      (6) (U//FOUO) Space, Cyber, and Information Integration.
         (a) Space: USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM coordinates space mission assurance; prioritizes critical space-enabled services (timing, comms, weather, ISR dissemination); and directs operational-level mitigation actions during coverage gaps (e.g., timing discipline, navigation risk management, alternate comm paths) consistent with JP 3-14.
         (b) Cyber: Defensive cyber operations (DCO) posture is elevated for the duration of MDIX. Cyber protection elements execute hunt/incident response drills; prioritize mission networks supporting C2 and logistics; and integrate cyber status into daily synchronization (JP 3-12).
         (c) Information: The joint force employs coordinated information activities to counter misinformation, preserve coalition cohesion, and support de-escalatory messaging consistent with policy (JP 3-13). Public affairs guidance is coordinated through JTF channels; OPSEC is enforced.

      (7) (U//FOUO) Deception / Signature Management (Exercise-Appropriate).
         (a) Components implement emission control (EMCON) plans, camouflage/concealment, and administrative measures that reduce signature and pattern predictability consistent with safety and host-nation requirements.
         (b) Deception activities are limited to exercise-appropriate measures approved by EXCON and consistent with policy; they are focused on complicating OPFOR ISR “confidence” and validating friendly battle drills, not on real-world misrepresentation.

4. (U//FOUO) FIRES (Targeting Priorities; ROE Constraints).

   a. (U//FOUO) Fires Intent (Exercise). Fires integration during MDIX is focused on joint process validation (JP 3-0; JP 3-30) and defensive denial demonstrations, with simulated effects in lieu of real-world target engagement. The objective is to validate the joint targeting cycle mechanics, sensor-to-decision pathways under degraded comms, and component coordination for dynamic retasking—without nominating real-world targets.

   b. (U//FOUO) Targeting Priorities (Simulated/Exercise-Controlled).
      (1) Protect the force and key nodes: prioritize simulated counter-ISR, defensive counterair, and IAMD-related effects that reduce OPFOR kill-chain confidence against distributed nodes and logistics movements.
      (2) Preserve C2 and sustainment: prioritize effects that maintain freedom of maneuver in the information environment and protect logistics distribution (e.g., simulated suppression of hostile sensing, simulated maritime denial in designated exercise areas).
      (3) Enable decision advantage: prioritize effects that restore/maintain ISR dissemination and communications pathways (including non-kinetic options and procedural mitigations).

   c. (U//FOUO) ROE / SRUF Constraints (Exercise).
      (1) All activities remain below armed conflict threshold; comply with SRUF, host-nation restrictions, and EXCON safety rules.
      (2) No real-world kinetic engagement authorities are granted by this OPLAN. Any weapons employment, if conducted at all, is limited to approved training events in designated ranges/areas with separate safety and clearance procedures.
      (3) Information activities and cyber operations are defensive and exercise-authorized; any offensive cyber effects are simulated by EXCON.

   d. (U//FOUO) Joint Targeting Process (Exercise Validation).
      (1) JTF validates a joint targeting working group (JTWG) battle rhythm for deliberate and dynamic targeting simulations, emphasizing: degraded communications read-backs, alternate data paths, and documentation discipline.
      (2) Measures of effectiveness include: time to produce a coordinated effects plan; accuracy and completeness of target development artifacts (exercise-only); and ability to retask based on changing OPFOR posture and logistics constraints.

5. (U//FOUO) FORCE SIZING (Narrative Apportionment and Required Capabilities by Domain).

   (U//FOUO) Note: To avoid providing actionable real-world deployment direction, this section describes notional force packages by type and scale appropriate for MDIX objectives. Specific unit names, exact quantities, and operating locations will be assigned in a separate EXORD/Annex A (Task Organization) and Annex C (Operations) under appropriate access controls and host-nation coordination.

   a. (U//FOUO) Air Domain Forces Required.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Tactical Fighter Forces. MDIX requires two notional fighter wings (each on the order of 18–24 multi-role fighters) distributed across one MOB and multiple FOS/CLs to validate dispersed sortie generation, DCA procedures, and dynamic retasking. These forces execute DCA-like and maritime strike simulation support (no target-specific planning), and provide agile combat employment (ACE) training events including rapid turn, hot-pit refuel (where authorized), and cross-servicing drills. A smaller partner detachment (4–8 fighters) may integrate for interoperability and shared airspace control procedures subject to releasability.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Bomber/Long-Range Aviation (Optional Inject). If apportioned, a notional bomber squadron package (6–8 aircraft) operates from an out-of-theater or rear-area MOB to validate long-range mission planning under degraded space services, including timing discipline and alternate comm pathways. Employment is limited to simulated effects and range-approved training.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Airborne C2/Relay. At least one airborne C2 platform detachment and one communications relay capability are required to bridge comm gaps and validate PACE. This package supports airspace control, maritime integration, and the ATO execution during SATCOM outages.
      (4) (U//FOUO) ISR Aviation. A mix of manned ISR and maritime patrol platforms (a squadron-equivalent package) is required to support maritime domain awareness, logistics threat indications/warnings, and OPFOR kill-chain simulations. The ISR plan will emphasize transport-denied conditions and alternate dissemination methods.
      (5) (U//FOUO) Air Mobility. One airlift wing-equivalent capability (a mix of strategic/tactical airlift sorties) is required to sustain distributed nodes, execute time-sensitive resupply, reposition personnel/equipment, and conduct aeromedical evacuation drills. Air mobility planning will explicitly include degraded PNT and contested airfield operations (procedural approaches and conservative risk controls).
      (6) (U//FOUO) Tanker Support. A rotational tanker detachment is required to enable extended-range sorties and repositioning. Tanker planning includes comm-out rendezvous procedures and conservative fuel reserves under navigation uncertainty.
      (7) (U//FOUO) Integrated Air and Missile Defense Enablers. A package of sensors and command elements (notional) is required to validate reporting and coordination in support of DCA/IAMD simulations, including procedural fallback for track sharing.

   b. (U//FOUO) Maritime Domain Forces Required.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Carrier Strike Group (CSG) or Equivalent Sea-Based Air. MDIX benefits from one CSG (or equivalent sea-based air package) to provide mobile aviation, sea control training, and an afloat C2 node resilient to shore node disruption. The associated carrier air wing scale is typically 40–50 aircraft. Operating areas are designated exercise sea areas in the Western Pacific, adjusted by EXCON to ensure safety and deconfliction.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Surface Action Group / Destroyer Squadron. At least one destroyer squadron-sized force (4–6 guided-missile destroyers) is required to train distributed maritime operations, escort/screening, and integration with the air picture under data link degradation. These ships operate across multiple sea areas to stress OPFOR ISR allocation and validate EMCON and reporting discipline.

One to two replenishment oilers and/or fast sealift elements (exercise-appropriate) are required to validate contested replenishment planning, alternate routing, and sustainment under threat. Actual movements will be coordinated for safety and policy compliance.

6. (U//FOUO) LOGISTICS (JP 4-0).

   a. (U//FOUO) Logistics Intent. Sustain distributed operations for seven days under persistent disruption while demonstrating the ability to (1) prioritize limited lift, (2) re-route around disrupted nodes, (3) operate without full digital logistics systems, and (4) maintain readiness through disciplined consumption and maintenance recovery.

   b. (U//FOUO) Concept of Support.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Priorities of Sustainment (generic order; JTF may adjust daily): (1) aviation and maritime fuel; (2) critical spares and munitions (training allocations); (3) medical and personnel support; (4) communications/cyber restoration materials; (5) base life support.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Distribution. Use a hub-and-spoke concept with multiple small spokes and pre-identified alternates. Exercise will include controlled injects that force closure or degradation of a primary node; logistics will respond via alternate nodes, split loads, variable timing, and alternate modes (air, sea, intra-theater surface).
      (3) (U//FOUO) Contested Logistics Battle Drills. Each component will rehearse: rapid reallocation of stocks; manual reporting when logistics IT is degraded; convoy/airlift mission re-planning under comms loss; and cross-servicing agreements for fuel and limited spares.
      (4) (U//FOUO) Maintenance and Readiness. Emphasize forward maintenance capability sized for dispersed operations (minimal essential test equipment, cannibalization controls, and fly-away kits). Measure readiness recovery after displacement and comm/cyber events.
      (5) (U//FOUO) Medical. Establish distributed Role 1/Role 2 coverage commensurate with exercise events; plan for aeromedical evacuation under comms degradation using pre-briefed routing and patient movement requests via alternate channels.
      (6) (U//FOUO) Contracting and Host-Nation Support. J4 coordinates contracting/host-nation support per permissions. Exercise includes injects that reduce contracted support to force adaptation and internal capability use.
      (7) (U//FOUO) Reporting. J4 publishes a daily sustainment SITREP format with a manual fallback. Metrics include: time-to-redirect shipment; time-to-restore minimum comms; fuel days-of-supply by node (coarse bands); sortie sustainment impacts; and maintenance turnaround.

   c. (U//FOUO) Risk Management. Logistics operations will balance dispersion with safety and force protection. Where comms degradation increases navigation or airfield/port risk, commanders will adopt conservative thresholds and use procedural control measures. EXCON retains authority to pause events for safety.

7. (U//FOUO) COMMAND AND CONTROL (JP 3-0; JP 3-30; JP 3-52; JP 3-12; JP 3-14).

   a. (U//FOUO) Command Relationships.
      (1) (U//FOUO) CDRUSINDOPACOM exercises COCOM through JTF-MDIX (exercise construct). Functional components (JFACC, JFMCC, JFLCC, JFSOCC) are established for MDIX with supporting/supporting relationships specified in the EXORD and component orders.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Supported Commander for Airspace Control. JFACC is designated Airspace Control Authority (ACA) for MDIX execution unless otherwise directed; JFMCC and JFLCC support with airspace coordination requirements (JP 3-52).
      (3) (U//FOUO) Cyber/Space Coordination. USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM provides space coordination and mission assurance; cyber forces provide DCO support. Coordination occurs through established cells embedded in the JTF battle rhythm.

   b. (U//FOUO) C2 Concept (Resilient Mission Command).
      (1) (U//FOUO) PACE Communications Plan. The JTF employs layered communications pathways: primary digital/SATCOM; alternate terrestrial networks (where available) and HF; contingency line-of-sight relay via airborne/ground assets; emergency courier/read-back procedures and pre-briefed execution matrices. Components will rehearse transition triggers and restoration procedures daily.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Degraded-Communications Battle Drills. Each component maintains a comm-out checklist: (a) execute last lawful order for a defined period; (b) shift to pre-briefed decision matrix; (c) attempt recontact via alternate; (d) report status upon restoration. These drills are validated through EXCON injects.
      (3) (U//FOUO) Battle Rhythm. Daily cycle includes: JTF update brief; JSM; ATO/ACO coordination events; LSB; cyber/space synchronization huddle; and end-of-day assessment. During comms outages, the JTF uses pre-scheduled windows and procedural check-ins.

   c. (U//FOUO) Information Management / Knowledge Management.
      (1) (U//FOUO) Establish minimum essential information set (MEIS) for degraded operations: friendly posture status bands, logistics status bands, airspace control changes, safety notices, and CCIR.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Implement releasability controls for allied/partner sharing; provide “sanitized common operating picture” products when full ISR feeds are unavailable.

   d. (U//FOUO) Assessment and Reporting.
      (1) (U//FOUO) J7 leads assessment with measures tied to end state: comms outage resilience, logistics reroute time, airspace control continuity, cross-domain coordination quality, and cyber/space incident response timeliness.
      (2) (U//FOUO) Capture capability/interoperability gaps suitable for CJCSI 3170.01 pathways, including urgent cross-domain data standards, manual fallback training gaps, and logistics IT resilience shortfalls.

8. (U//FOUO) COORDINATING INSTRUCTIONS.

   a. (U//FOUO) Safety and Deconfliction. All components comply with EXCON safety controls, range regulations, and civil deconfliction requirements. When in doubt, safety overrides training objectives.

   b. (U//FOUO) OPSEC. Do not disseminate sensitive movement or posture details beyond authorized channels. Use approved exercise cover terms where applicable.

   c. (U//FOUO) Legal/Policy. Ensure operations conform to SRUF, host-nation restrictions, and applicable law. Cyber and information activities remain defensive and exercise-authorized.

   d. (U//FOUO) Environmental and Navigational Compliance. Maritime and air operations comply with environmental rules and safe navigation practices; no exercise activity will create real-world hazards to navigation or civil aviation.

9. (U//FOUO) ADMINISTRATION AND LOGISTICS (Administrative).

   a. (U//FOUO) Personnel Accountability. Components report daily personnel accountability status through established channels, with manual backup during IT outages.

   b. (U//FOUO) Medical Reporting. Report incidents and medical events per theater medical SOP. Exercise includes simulated mass casualty injects; real-world response remains primary.

   c. (U//FOUO) Public Affairs. All public release coordinated through JTF PAO and consistent with approved themes/messages; counter-misinformation responses coordinated with information activities cell per JP 3-13.

10. (U//FOUO) COMMAND.

   a. (U//FOUO) Command Posts. JTF maintains primary and alternate C2 nodes with COOP procedures; components identify alternate nodes and minimal manning for continuity.

   b. (U//FOUO) Succession of Command. As published in JTF-MDIX EXORD and component orders.

11. (U//FOUO) SUMMARY.

This OPLAN provides operational-level direction to execute MDIX 01–08 MAR 2026 in INDOPACOM’s Western Pacific theater to validate distributed posture, resilient C2 under degraded space services, integrated joint air-maritime-space-cyber operations, and contested logistics sustainment. Components will execute phased objectives, prioritize safety and policy compliance, and capture lessons learned and capability gaps consistent with JP 5-0 and CJCSI 3170.01 pathways.
