MOE-P2.2 Air tasking disruption: At least one daily period (minimum 2 hours) where adversary air C2 is assessed “degraded” (delayed tasking, reduced coordination) due to simulated effects.
MOE-P2.3 Blue counterair dominance: Blue achieves favorable simulated exchange ratio in air-to-air adjudication events during W1/W2 while maintaining CAP continuity.

PRIORITY 3 (P3) — Maritime Power Projection

MOE-P3.2 Kill-chain disruption: On at least 4 days (Days 4–8), break the adversary maritime reconnaissance-to-strike sequence (cueing disrupted, targeting delayed, or engagement denied) as evidenced by ISR/cyber/EMS assessment.
MOE-P3.3 Joint integration: Execute at least one coordinated event per day where air sorties provide cueing/confirmation for simulated DDG/SSN fires (timed within 10 minutes of planned window).

MOE-P4.2 Resilient C2: Successfully execute at least two mission packages (Days 6–8) with planned autonomy—no real-time updates required—while still meeting timing and deconfliction constraints.
MOE-P4.3 ISR characterization: Produce daily fused assessment of adversary network activity (from RC-135 and space ISR injects) with actionable recommendations for the next day’s allocation.

MOE-P5.3 Logistics corridor assurance: Demonstrate that air operations continue at planned sortie rates despite two or more contested logistics injects (fuel/munitions/maintenance constraints), with recovery to within 85% of planned capacity within 24 hours of each inject.

DAILY ASSESSMENT RHYTHM (to drive next ATO)
- +2 hours after W1: quick-look P1/P2 effects and corridor status for same-day adjustments (within limits).
- +2 hours after W2: preliminary daily MOE roll-up; identify refly needs and dynamic target nominations (exercise).

{
  "title": "Joint Strategic Capabilities Plan (JSCP) — INDOPACOM Western Pacific Multi-Domain Integration Exercise (MDIX) and Contested Logistics/Degraded Space Readiness (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026)",
  "docType": "JSCP",
  "authorityLevel": "CJCS",
  "content": "MEMORANDUM FOR: Commander, United States Indo-Pacific Command

FROM: Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

SUBJECT: Joint Strategic Capabilities Plan (JSCP) — INDOPACOM Western Pacific Multi-Domain Integration Exercise (MDIX) and Contested Logistics/Degraded Space Readiness (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026)

DATE: 01 MAR 2026

CLASSIFICATION: UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO


1. PURPOSE.

   a. This Joint Strategic Capabilities Plan (JSCP) provides tasking and apportionment guidance to Commander, United States Indo-Pacific Command (CDRUSINDOPACOM) for the 01–08 MAR 2026 Western Pacific multi-domain integration exercise window and for follow-on planning actions required to institutionalize readiness under contested logistics and degraded/intermittent space-enabled services. This JSCP converts the theater military objectives and strategic lines of effort in the parent authority into specific combatant command (CCMD) tasks and planning requirements consistent with joint doctrine (JP 5-0, Joint Planning; JP 3-0, Joint Campaigns and Operations).

   b. Parent Authority and Derivation. This JSCP is explicitly derived from and implements the “National Military Strategy (NMS) Theater Annex — INDOPACOM / Western Pacific Integrated Deterrence and Multi-Domain Readiness (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026),” dated 01 MAR 2026, UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO (hereafter “NMS Theater Annex”). The NMS Theater Annex is itself derived from the “National Defense Strategy (NDS) Extract — Western Pacific Integrated Deterrence and Multi-Domain Readiness (INDOPACOM) (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026),” dated 01 MAR 2026, UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO. Where tension exists, the NMS Theater Annex remains the controlling parent authority for theater strategic intent during this window; this JSCP provides execution-enabling tasking and planning direction to USINDOPACOM and supporting components.

   c. Scope. This JSCP:
      (1) Establishes campaign objectives for USINDOPACOM (per JP 5-0) aligned to the NMS Theater Annex strategic priorities (DENY, DEGRADE, PROTECT, SUSTAIN, DESTROY).
      (2) Provides force allocation priorities and apportionment guidance for the exercise window, including force sizing targets to enable realistic downstream planning.
      (3) Directs planning products (OPLANs/CONPLANs and supporting plans) focused on distributed operations, resilient command and control (C2), contested logistics, and degraded space support.
      (4) Directs coordination requirements with supporting components, subordinate unified commands (if applicable), adjacent CCMDs (EUCOM and CENTCOM), U.S. Cyber Command (USCYBERCOM) for coordination, and U.S. Space Command (USSPACECOM) and U.S. Space Forces–Indo-Pacific for integration.
      (5) Establishes assessment expectations to inform follow-on force posture and capability refinement, consistent with JP 5-0 and JP 3-0.

   d. Operational Assumptions (Baseline for Planning). In accordance with the NMS Theater Annex (Strategic Environment, paras. 2a–2d), assume:
      (1) Contested logistics as a continuous condition (JP 4-0, Joint Logistics).
      (2) Intermittent SATCOM, localized PNT degradation, and ISR transport gaps as routine (JP 3-14, Space Operations).
      (3) Persistent EMS and cyber contestation affecting C2, sensing, and logistics systems (JP 3-12, Cyberspace Operations; JP 3-13, Information).
      (4) A near-peer adversary employing calibrated coercion below the threshold of armed conflict, rapid escalation options, and a mature long-range precision strike complex.


2. STRATEGIC ENVIRONMENT.

   a. Reference. The strategic environment for this JSCP is as described in the parent authority “NMS Theater Annex — INDOPACOM / Western Pacific Integrated Deterrence and Multi-Domain Readiness (Effective 01–08 MAR 2026),” dated 01 MAR 2026, UNCLASSIFIED // FOUO, paragraphs 2–3. This JSCP operationalizes the NMS Theater Annex assessment that degraded space support and contested logistics are baseline planning conditions in the Western Pacific rather than episodic disruptions.

   b. Adversary Context (Near-Peer, Pacific). The adversary is assessed to possess:
      (1) A2/AD systems capable of threatening ports, airfields, logistics hubs, and distributed basing nodes across the First and Second Island Chains.
      (2) Mature counterspace and cyber capabilities intended to degrade SATCOM, PNT, ISR dissemination, and data integrity.
      (3) Integrated maritime-air long-range precision strike and robust ISR to enable dynamic targeting against mobile and fixed nodes.
      (4) Information operations intended to undermine coalition cohesion, create decision paralysis, and shape escalation narratives (JP 3-13).

   c. Implications for Joint Force Employment. In alignment with JP 3-0 and the NMS Theater Annex (para. 2d), USINDOPACOM must plan and operate with:
      (1) Distributed operations requiring mission-type orders and rehearsed battle drills for communications loss (JP 5-0).
      (2) Multiple, interoperable C2 pathways (primary/alternate/contingency/emergency), including line-of-sight and terrestrial relay options where feasible.
      (3) Logistics designs prioritizing dispersion, deception, redundancy, rapid reconstitution, and protected distribution (JP 4-0).
      (4) Integrated air-maritime-space-cyber planning to sustain decision advantage and deny a rapid fait accompli (JP 3-0; JP 3-30, Joint Air Operations; JP 3-52, Joint Airspace Control).


3. STRATEGIC PRIORITIES (TASKING, EFFECTS, AND DOCTRINAL JUSTIFICATION).

   CDRUSINDOPACOM will execute the following tasks and develop the required plans to achieve the effects directed by the NMS Theater Annex. These priorities are mutually supporting and will be integrated into USINDOPACOM campaigning and the 01–08 MAR 2026 exercise design.

   3.1. DENY (Theater Effect): Deny the adversary the ability to achieve a rapid fait accompli or coercive objectives in the Western Pacific by sustaining combat-credible, distributed posture and assured freedom of maneuver across domains.

      a. USINDOPACOM Campaign Objectives (JP 5-0).
         (1) Maintain a distributed, responsive posture that can transition from steady-state presence to crisis-action dispersion without loss of operational tempo.
         (2) Demonstrate freedom of navigation and overflight, and preserve operational access to key terrain and approaches consistent with international law.
         (3) Validate the ability to concentrate effects rapidly from dispersed positions while complicating adversary targeting.

      b. Tasks to CDRUSINDOPACOM.
         (1) Establish a theater-wide Distributed Posture and Maneuver Framework for 01–08 MAR 2026 that identifies: (a) primary and alternate operating locations; (b) deception, emissions control (EMCON), and mobility concepts; and (c) decision thresholds for dispersion/concentration. Ensure framework is feasible under intermittent SATCOM and degraded PNT (JP 3-0; JP 5-0; JP 3-14).
         (2) Direct component commanders (PACFLT, PACAF, MARFORPAC, USARPAC, USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM) to rehearse mission-type orders and degraded communications battle drills in the exercise scenario, including delegated authorities and preplanned responses to loss of data links and ISR feeds (JP 5-0).
         (3) Integrate joint air and maritime denial demonstrations (defensive counterair, maritime strike coordination, undersea integration where available) to show credible denial without creating single-point dependencies on major hubs (JP 3-30; JP 3-0).

      c. Apportionment and Force Allocation Priorities (DENY).
         (1) First priority: air and maritime forces enabling rapid defensive response and maritime denial (fighter squadrons, surface combatants, submarines where apportioned, maritime patrol).
         (2) Second priority: joint C2 and data transport resilience (airborne C2, relay, and tactical data link gateways; terrestrial and line-of-sight alternatives).
         (3) Third priority: expeditionary basing and security forces to enable austere operations and node defense.

      d. Justification. JP 3-0 identifies denial of adversary objectives and preservation of freedom of action as central to campaigning in contested environments; JP 3-30 and JP 3-52 emphasize integrated air operations and airspace control as prerequisites to maneuver and protection in contested airspace. The NMS Theater Annex (Priority 3.1) requires distributed posture and assured freedom of maneuver to deny coercion.


   3.2. DEGRADE (Theater Effect): Degrade adversary kill chains, ISR, and C2—especially counterspace, cyber, and long-range precision-strike enabling functions—through resilience, deception, and layered defense.

      a. USINDOPACOM Campaign Objectives (JP 5-0).
         (1) Reduce adversary targeting confidence through dispersion, signature management, deception, and rapid reconstitution.
         (2) Preserve decision advantage despite cyber/EMS attack and intermittent space support.
         (3) Increase survivability of C2 nodes and theater sustainment nodes by redundancy, mobility, and integrated defensive measures.

      b. Tasks to CDRUSINDOPACOM.
         (1) Publish and exercise a Theater Resilient C2 Concept of Operations (CONOPS) for intermittent SATCOM and data transport gaps, to include: data prioritization; minimum essential information requirements; cross-domain and releasability procedures for coalition sharing; and “offline-by-design” fallback processes (JP 5-0; JP 3-14; JP 3-0).
         (2) Coordinate with USSPACECOM and USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM to integrate space mission assurance measures into operational design (alternate PNT procedures, protected SATCOM options where available, and ISR dissemination workarounds). Ensure exercise injects include localized PNT degradation and SATCOM denial episodes (JP 3-14).
         (3) Coordinate with USCYBERCOM (for coordination) to prioritize defensive cyber operations (DCO) and incident response for mission systems supporting: (a) C2; (b) logistics IT and in-transit visibility; (c) air tasking/airspace control systems; and (d) base defense and IAMD integration interfaces (JP 3-12; JP 4-0; JP 3-52).
         (4) Direct component commanders to integrate deception and signature management into daily battle rhythm (movement timing variability, EMCON adherence, decoy employment where feasible, and operational security discipline), measured through exercise assessment.

      c. Apportionment and Force Allocation Priorities (DEGRADE).
         (1) First priority: cyber protection teams / mission defense teams (where available) focused on logistics and C2; EMS resilience measures and electronic protection.
         (2) Second priority: space support coordination elements and space mission assurance enablers (planning expertise, operational procedures, alternate comm paths).
         (3) Third priority: capabilities enabling rapid reconstitution of C2 and sensing (deployable comm packages, gateway/relay, expeditionary network kits).

      d. Justification. The NMS Theater Annex (Priority 3.2) directs resilience and degradation of adversary kill chains as a strategic imperative. JP 3-12 and JP 3-14 direct mission assurance and operational integration under contested cyber/space conditions; JP 5-0 emphasizes establishing branches and sequels for degraded connectivity and ensuring feasibility.


   3.3. PROTECT (Theater Effect): Protect U.S. forces, treaty allies and partners, critical nodes, and the global commons by reinforcing collective defense, integrated air and missile defense (IAMD), airspace control, and secure lines of communication.

      a. USINDOPACOM Campaign Objectives (JP 5-0).
         (1) Improve joint/combined airspace control and air defense integration to reduce fratricide risk and protect key nodes.
         (2) Protect air and maritime lines of communication for reinforcement and sustainment.
         (3) Reduce vulnerability of bases, ports, and logistics nodes via integrated active and passive defense.

      b. Tasks to CDRUSINDOPACOM.
         (1) Direct development and exercise validation of a Joint/Combined Airspace Control Plan (ACP) and Air Defense Plan (ADP) suitable for degraded communications and intermittent link availability, including common identification procedures, procedural control measures, and fallback authorities (JP 3-52; JP 3-30).
         (2) In coordination with PACFLT and relevant interagency partners as appropriate, rehearse protection of sea lines of communication (SLOC) and critical maritime infrastructure awareness measures, including escort concepts for high-value logistics movements and port throughput continuity actions (JP 3-0; JP 4-0).
         (3) Ensure passive defense measures (dispersal, camouflage, concealment, deception, hardening where available) are integrated into base and port defense plans and are exercised as opposed to remaining notional (JP 3-0; JP 3-52).
         (4) Coordinate with allies and partners, consistent with treaties, SOFAs, access arrangements, and releasability constraints referenced in the NMS Theater Annex (para. 3.3c), to expand combined planning and information sharing for air and maritime picture integration during the exercise window.

      c. Apportionment and Force Allocation Priorities (PROTECT).
         (1) First priority: IAMD and air defense command and control capabilities (to include sensors, command nodes, and fighter defensive counterair capacity).
         (2) Second priority: base defense, expeditionary security, EOD, and engineering for survivability and rapid repair.
         (3) Third priority: maritime protection assets supporting escort and area security for logistics movements, commensurate with risk.

      d. Justification. JP 3-0 defines protection as a core joint function required to maintain freedom of action; JP 3-52 emphasizes effective airspace control and integrated air defense to enable joint operations and reduce fratricide risk in complex, coalition airspace. The NMS Theater Annex (Priority 3.3) directs combined IAMD and secure lines of communication as essential to protecting allies and forward forces.


   3.4. SUSTAIN (Theater Effect): Sustain a distributed Joint Force by strengthening contested logistics, diversified access, distributed stocks, protected distribution, and the ability to fight through disruption.

      a. USINDOPACOM Campaign Objectives (JP 5-0).
         (1) Prevent culmination driven by interdiction, infrastructure loss, or supply chain/cyber disruption.
         (2) Validate logistics C2 and prioritization under degraded communications and cyber pressure.
         (3) Increase endurance of forward forces via prepositioning, distributed stockage, and expeditionary repair.

      b. Tasks to CDRUSINDOPACOM.
         (1) Direct establishment (or refinement) of a Theater Contested Logistics Concept of Support for 01–08 MAR 2026 that identifies prioritized commodities (fuel, critical munitions, key spares), minimum stock levels by node, and decision criteria for distribution re-routing under threat (JP 4-0; JP 5-0).
         (2) Exercise logistics C2 under comms degradation: require components to operate with intermittent connectivity to logistics IT systems and to execute manual/alternate reporting and prioritization procedures for in-transit visibility (JP 4-0; JP 3-14).
         (3) Integrate rapid airfield/port damage repair and throughput restoration injects (crater repair, MHE disruption, fuel system damage, cyber impacts to terminal operations) and require measurable restoration timelines (JP 4-0; JP 3-0).
         (4) Coordinate with TRANSCOM (supporting) through Joint Staff processes to validate intratheater distribution requirements and to identify lift shortfalls exposed by the exercise design (JP 4-0).
         (5) Identify top theater munitions and spares with low depth/high consumption risk and provide prioritized demand signals through the Joint Staff and Services consistent with CJCSI 3170.01 (Joint Capabilities Integration and Development System) and the NMS Theater Annex (para. 3.4e).

      c. Apportionment and Force Allocation Priorities (SUSTAIN).
         (1) First priority: intratheater lift, expeditionary logistics units, and sustainment enablers supporting dispersed nodes (fuel distribution, expeditionary maintenance, medical, engineering).
         (2) Second priority: protected distribution capabilities (escort coordination, route flexibility, deception support) and node defense enablers for logistics hubs.
         (3) Third priority: afloat/expeditionary repair and battle damage repair capabilities that restore sortie and throughput generation.

      d. Justification. JP 4-0 identifies logistics as foundational to operational reach and endurance and a primary target in peer conflict; JP 5-0 requires sustainment feasibility and risk to be integrated at plan inception. The NMS Theater Annex (Priority 3.4) elevates contested logistics to a theater strategic effect, requiring distributed nodes and fight-through sustainment.


   3.5. DESTROY (Theater Effect): Destroy adversary confidence in successful aggression by demonstrating credible, coalition-enabled capability to impose unacceptable costs and—if deterrence fails—defeat aggression and restore the status quo ante.

      a. USINDOPACOM Campaign Objectives (JP 5-0).
         (1) Demonstrate credible defeat mechanisms integrated across air, maritime, space, and cyber, capable of functioning through degraded ISR and communications.
         (2) Demonstrate rapid reinforcement and regeneration of combat power.
         (3) Integrate information discipline and strategic messaging to reinforce deterrence while managing escalation risk (JP 3-13).

      b. Tasks to CDRUSINDOPACOM.
         (1) Design and execute an exercise sequence that demonstrates cross-domain integration of maritime strike coordination, defensive counterair, and undersea/surface integration (as available), including degraded targeting inputs and alternate sensor-to-shooter pathways (JP 3-0; JP 3-30).
         (2) Coordinate with USSPACECOM and USCYBERCOM (for coordination) to demonstrate continuity of operations when space services are partially denied and when mission systems are under cyber pressure; assess operational impacts and identify procedural mitigations (JP 3-14; JP 3-12).
         (3) Ensure public affairs and information planning supports disciplined messaging, protects sensitive sources/methods, and counters adversary malign narratives targeting alliance cohesion, consistent with JP 3-13 and the NMS Theater Annex (paras. 2b(4) and 4b(6)).

      c. Apportionment and Force Allocation Priorities (DESTROY).
         (1) First priority: forces and enablers that create credible, observable capability to impose costs (maritime strike-capable air, surface combatants, undersea capabilities where apportioned, and associated ISR/EW).
         (2) Second priority: operational demonstrations of resilient C2 and sustainment that specifically reduce adversary confidence in exploiting degradation.
         (3) Third priority: coalition integration enablers (combined planning cells, liaison teams, releasable common operational picture pathways).

      d. Justification. JP 3-0 frames credible combat power and coherent objectives as the foundation of deterrence; JP 5-0 directs the translation of strategy into feasible plans with clear endstates and assessment. The NMS Theater Annex (Priority 3.5) requires credible defeat capability as the backstop to deterrence, demonstrated under degraded conditions rather than assumed.


4. COMMANDER’S INTENT (DERIVED FROM PARENT GUIDANCE).

   a. Purpose. Consistent with the NMS Theater Annex (Commander’s Intent, para. 4a), CDRUSINDOPACOM will strengthen integrated deterrence in the Western Pacific by demonstrating and institutionalizing multi-domain readiness that can fight through contested logistics and intermittent space-enabled services. This JSCP directs tasks to ensure the joint force can deny coercion, protect allies and forward forces, sustain distributed operations, degrade adversary kill chains, and destroy adversary confidence in a successful rapid aggression option.

   b. Method. CDRUSINDOPACOM will:
      (1) Employ a distributed posture and dynamic force employment to complicate adversary ISR/targeting while preserving the ability to concentrate effects rapidly (JP 3-0).
      (2) Execute resilient, interoperable C2 designed for degraded connectivity using mission-type orders, delegated authorities, and multiple communications pathways (JP 5-0).
      (3) Build and rehearse fight-through sustainment via diversified nodes, distributed stocks, protected distribution, expeditionary repair, and logistics C2 that can function under cyber and comms disruption (JP 4-0).
      (4) Integrate air-maritime-space-cyber capabilities to maintain decision advantage and degrade adversary kill chain effectiveness, with explicit procedures for operating under degraded PNT/ISR (JP 3-30; JP 3-14; JP 3-12).
      (5) Reinforce alliance and partner integration consistent with treaties, SOFAs, access arrangements, and releasability constraints as described in the NMS Theater Annex (para. 3.3c), emphasizing interoperability that survives degraded networks.
      (6) Manage escalation risk through disciplined messaging, adherence to law and policy, and clear distinction between readiness demonstration and conflict initiation (JP 3-0; JP 3-13).

   c. Planning Requirements (Directed Products and Timelines). To institutionalize the NMS Theater Annex priorities beyond the 01–08 MAR 2026 window, CDRUSINDOPACOM will develop or update the following planning products (titles may be refined; content requirements are directive):
      (1) CONPLAN – “WESTPAC Resilient C2 and Degraded Space Operations.” NLT 60 days after 08 MAR 2026, submit a commander-approved CONPLAN addressing: C2 architecture assumptions; alternate communications pathways; degraded PNT procedures; ISR dissemination workarounds; authorities/delegations; and battle drills for data loss. Must integrate space mission assurance coordination with USSPACECOM and USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM (JP 5-0; JP 3-14).
      (2) CONPLAN – “Contested Logistics and Distributed Sustainment (CLDS).” NLT 90 days after 08 MAR 2026, submit a commander-approved CONPLAN addressing: distributed stockage; diversified access; protected distribution; intratheater lift requirements; expeditionary maintenance/repair; medical dispersion; and logistics C2 under cyber/comms attack. Must include decision points and prioritization schema for fuel/munitions allocation during connectivity loss (JP 4-0; JP 5-0).
      (3) Supporting Plan – “Joint/Combined ACP/ADP Degraded Comms Annex.” NLT 45 days after 08 MAR 2026, publish a validated annex (or supporting plan) to the theater airspace control and air defense planning framework describing procedural control, common ID, and fallback measures under degraded communications, with coalition integration and releasability considerations (JP 3-52; JP 3-30).
      (4) Exercise After-Action Report (AAR) with DOTMLPF-P Recommendations. NLT 30 days after 08 MAR 2026, provide an AAR focused on: (a) C2 resilience; (b) logistics fight-through performance; (c) coalition interoperability under degraded networks; and (d) vulnerabilities discovered in cyber/space dependencies. Include prioritized recommendations suitable for CJCS and Service follow-up consistent with CJCSI 3170.01 processes.

   d. Force Allocation Priorities and Apportionment Guidance (01–08 MAR 2026 Window). In support of the NMS Theater Annex and the above tasks, apportionment priorities for this exercise window are:
      (1) Joint/combined C2 resilience and airspace/air defense integration (airborne C2, data link management, procedural control capability).
      (2) Maritime denial and protection of logistics movements (surface combatants, maritime patrol, and escort planning).
      (3) Expeditionary basing and sustainment enabling units (engineering, airfield opening/repair, fuel distribution, expeditionary maintenance).
      (4) ISR/EW support with explicit planning for ISR transport and dissemination gaps; collection plans must include “loss-of-coverage” branches (JP 3-0; JP 5-0).
      (5) Space and cyber mission assurance support (USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM integration; DCO and incident response priorities).

   e. Force Sizing Guidance (Planning Targets). For planning and exercise realism, CDRUSINDOPACOM will size forces to meet the targets below. These targets inform request for forces (RFF), joint manning, and supporting component alignment; they are not guarantees of allocation but are the baseline for feasibility analysis and risk articulation in submissions to the Joint Staff.
      (1) Naval Task Forces: Plan for 2 Carrier Strike Groups (CSGs) available within theater or immediately adjacent waters, and 1 Expeditionary Strike Group (ESG) or Amphibious Ready Group/Marine Expeditionary Unit (ARG/MEU) equivalent for expeditionary advanced basing and logistics support demonstration.
      (2) Air Forces: Plan for 10 fighter squadrons (mix of USAF/USN/USMC) capable of defensive counterair and maritime strike integration, with at least 2 squadrons operating from dispersed/austere locations under Agile Combat Employment (ACE) conditions.
      (3) Bomber Tasking: Plan for 2 bomber taskings (e.g., Bomber Task Force sorties) during the window, integrated into maritime strike/long-range targeting vignettes with degraded ISR injects.
      (4) Tanking: Plan for 4 tanker orbits (or equivalent capacity) to sustain distributed operations, recognizing threat-driven orbit displacement and intermittent connectivity.
      (5) ISR/EW: Plan for 6 ISR/EW support taskings (manned and unmanned as available), explicitly including at least 2 events with ISR dissemination/transport disruption and alternate exploitation/dissemination procedures.
      (6) Expeditionary Logistics/Engineering: Plan for at least 2 expeditionary airfield/port damage repair packages and 2 expeditionary fuel distribution elements to support dispersed nodes.
      (7) Space/Cyber: Plan for continuous integration of a space support coordination element and prioritized DCO/incident response support to mission systems identified in paragraph 3.2b(3).

   f. Coordination with Adjacent CCMDs and Supporting Commands.
      (1) USCENTCOM. Coordinate to deconflict high-demand/low-density assets (tankers, ISR, missile defense, cyber protection teams) and ensure global force management alignment for surge or diversion scenarios affecting INDOPACOM sustainment routes and munitions flows.
      (2) USEUCOM. Coordinate to ensure availability and deconfliction for strategic lift, bomber tasking sourcing, and space/cyber effects synchronization that may require global posture considerations.
      (3) USTRANSCOM (supporting). Coordinate to validate lift feasibility, contested distribution alternatives, and port/airfield throughput assumptions used in CLDS planning (JP 4-0).
      (4) USSPACECOM (supporting) and USSPACEFOR–INDOPACOM (theater component). Coordinate to integrate space mission assurance, SATCOM prioritization, alternate PNT procedures, and space-related incident reporting within exercise battle rhythm (JP 3-14).
      (5) USCYBERCOM (for coordination). Coordinate defensive cyber priorities, incident response timelines, and mission assurance assessments for C2 and logistics systems (JP 3-12).

   g. Acceptable Risk. In accordance with the NMS Theater Annex (para. 4d), accept prudent risk in operational demonstration and distributed posture to achieve readiness and signaling benefits. Do not accept risk that creates single points of failure in C2 or sustainment, or that undermines alliance cohesion. Explicitly document risk acceptance decisions and mitigation measures in all required plans (JP 5-0).


5. ENDSTATE.

   a. Desired Endstate (01–08 MAR 2026 and Enduring). Derived directly from the NMS Theater Annex (Endstate, para. 5), the endstate for this JSCP is achieved when USINDOPACOM demonstrates and can sustain a credible, coalition-enabled, multi-domain readiness posture in the Western Pacific in which:
      (1) The adversary is deterred from coercion and rapid aggression due to credible denial, protection, and defeat mechanisms that function under contested logistics and intermittent space support.
      (2) Joint and combined forces maintain operational tempo and decision advantage through planned SATCOM outages, PNT degradation, and ISR dissemination gaps, using redundant pathways, mission-type orders, and rehearsed degraded-mode procedures.
      (3) Distributed basing and sustainment are validated through measurable performance: continued sortie/mission generation from multiple locations, restored throughput after damage injects, and effective rerouting of supplies during disruption (JP 4-0).
      (4) Joint/combined airspace control and air defense integration reduces fratricide risk and protects critical nodes, with procedural fallback measures proven under degraded communications (JP 3-52).
      (5) Alliance and partner interoperability is measurably improved through validated combined planning products, rehearsed information sharing within releasability constraints, and credible host-nation support/access integration.
      (6) USINDOPACOM provides actionable, prioritized DOTMLPF-P recommendations and capability demand signals (CJCSI 3170.01) based on exercise-validated gaps in contested logistics and space/cyber mission assurance.

   b. Measures of Effectiveness (MOE) and Reporting. CDRUSINDOPACOM will assess and report (via the AAR directed in paragraph 4c(4)) at minimum:
      (1) C2 Resilience: ability to execute essential C2 functions during scripted SATCOM/PNT degradations with documented workarounds and decision timelines.
      (2) Sustainment Endurance: success in maintaining distributed operations with disrupted in-transit visibility and contested distribution, including time-to-restore for damaged nodes.
      (3) Protection Integration: effectiveness of airspace control and air defense integration under degraded communications, including identification discipline and procedural control effectiveness.
      (4) Coalition Integration: number and quality of combined planning artifacts validated; interoperability under degraded networks; and constraints requiring policy/technical mitigation.

   c. Force Sizing Table (Planning Targets for MDIX 01–08 MAR 2026).
      * Required fighter squadrons: 10
      * Required bomber taskings: 2
      * Required CSG/ESG: 3 (2 CSG, 1 ESG/ARG equivalent)
      * Required ISR/EW support: 6
      * Required tanker orbits: 4

BATTLE DAMAGE ASSESSMENT (BDA) REPORT – DAY 1 OPERATIONS (PHASE 0: SHAPE)
THEATER: INDOPACOM / WESTERN PACIFIC
ADVERSARY: NEAR-PEER STATE (PACIFIC)
DTG: DAY 1 (LOCAL)

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

1.1. Overall Assessment. Day 1 operations achieved the Phase 0 intent: demonstrate credible defensive posture, expand multi-INT situational awareness, and characterize key adversary ISR/IADS/C2 and maritime sensor networks without crossing escalation thresholds. No confirmed kinetic effects were generated; effects were predominantly informational (collection) and behavioral (deterrence/posture).

1.2. Mission Effectiveness. DCA/CAP coverage met required presence and response timelines for simulated HVAs and CSG operating area. ISR sorties (RC-135V and F-35A) produced meaningful updates to emitter libraries and preliminary pattern-of-life for “RED SHIELD-N,” “RED SKY-3,” and “RED NET-A.” Maritime picture quality improved modestly; adversary surface radar clusters “RED WAVE-2” and SAG indicator set “RED FLOT-1” remain only partially resolved due to intermittent emissions and adversary emission control (EMCON).

1.3. Adversary Reaction (Observed/Assessed). Adversary responded with disciplined, time-bounded radar activations, apparent comms routing changes within “RED NET-A,” and increased reliance on passive sensors. No adversary manned ISR aircraft successfully penetrated simulated defense core; however, overhead collection threat remained persistent (robust SAR/EO/ELINT constellation) and likely collected on friendly airborne posture, tanker tracks, and any non-essential emissions.

1.4. Key Limitations. Space/SATCOM degradation (selected TDRS and WGS nodes degraded) created intermittent bandwidth constraints for timely cross-cueing and near-real-time PED dissemination. Maritime detection/ID gaps persisted due to adversary EMCON, weather/sea state impacts on certain phenomenologies, and limited dwell time on suspected operating boxes.

1.5. Bottom Line. Day 1 was effective for shaping and ISR characterization; insufficient for claiming decisive degradation of any adversary capability except limited, localized, temporary reduction in the simulated SA-XX battery’s engagement efficiency (assessed via SEAD rehearsal effects and adversary emission behavior). Priority for next cycle: deepen fix/track/target continuity on mobile IADS and maritime sensors, and map “RED NET-A” routing and node hierarchy to enable rapid transition to Phase 1+ options if directed.

2. TARGET-BY-TARGET ASSESSMENT

Note: In Phase 0, “damage” is assessed as (a) physical damage where applicable, (b) functional degradation if simulated electronic/cyber/SEAD effects were applied, and/or (c) “information gain” against the target set when the objective was characterize/locate/monitor. Percentages reflect estimated mission effect against the desired end state for the target (not necessarily physical destruction).

2.1. ADV IADS SECTOR RED SHIELD-N (SIM) – AIR_DEFENSE
- Platform(s) Employed: RIVET 31/32 (RC-135V SIGINT/ELINT); FALCON 61 (F-35A passive sensing); SENTRY 71/72 (E-3G C2 for intercept management); supporting CAP packages for force protection.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 65% (characterize/locate objective progress).
- Functional Impact: Improved emitter ID confidence and sector boundary refinement; preliminary association of search/acquisition emitters to command relationships. Adversary reaction indicated tighter emission windows and possible decoy/alternate emitters, suggesting they detected collection pressure.
- Re-strike Recommendation: NO (kinetic) / YES (collection continuation). Justification: Objective is characterization; additional multi-INT passes required to raise geolocation accuracy and confirm mobile components and sector handoff procedures.

2.2. NAVAL SURFACE SEARCH RADAR CLUSTERS RED WAVE-2 (SIM) – NAVAL
- Platform(s) Employed: RIVET 31/32; BLADE 31 and HAMMER 51/52 (F/A-18E patrol/ESM support); space ISR/SAR/EO as available (friendly commercial/DoD ISR listed operational).
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 45% (locate/report objective progress).
- Functional Impact: Partial mapping of radar cluster presence and operating rhythm; insufficient classification fidelity to separate all contributors (coastal installations vs embarked emitters) when adversary used burst transmissions and frequency agility.
- Re-strike Recommendation: YES (ISR) / NO (kinetic). Justification: Maritime radar cluster remains a critical enabler for adversary MDA and targeting; requires persistent collection and cross-cueing to establish reliable geo-fixes and differentiate emitters.

2.3. ADV COASTAL EARLY WARNING RADAR RED SKY-3 (SIM) – AIR_DEFENSE
- Platform(s) Employed: RIVET 31/32; FALCON 61; escort provided by PANTHER 11/12; DCA cover VIPER 21/22, RAZOR 31, SENTINEL 11/12 as required.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 70% (persistent detection/characterize objective progress).
- Functional Impact: Achieved consistent detection of radar activations with improved parameter characterization. Assessed adversary implemented EMCON and/or shifted to alternate sensor nodes during known collection windows.
- Re-strike Recommendation: YES (ISR). Justification: Continue to build pattern-of-life, validate alternate site usage, and refine geolocation to support future targetable solutions if posture escalates.

2.4. LINK/COMMS NODES RED NET-A (SIM) – C2
- Platform(s) Employed: RIVET 31/32 SIGINT; SENTRY 71/72 for tactical C2 picture correlation; friendly protected SATCOM (AEHF/MUOS) supported own-force resilience; limited exploitation due to bandwidth constraints.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 55% (identify/monitor objective progress).
- Functional Impact: Identified probable node hierarchy (primary/alternate) and traffic volume changes coincident with friendly CAP/ISR surges; suggests adversary routing discipline and possible use of low probability of intercept techniques. No confirmed functional disruption imposed.
- Re-strike Recommendation: YES (collection and cyber prep) / NO (kinetic). Justification: RED NET-A is pivotal for IADS/maritime cueing; additional mapping required to identify critical nodes, redundancy, and potential choke points.

2.5. DCA COVERAGE HVA (SIM) – C2 (Deterrence/Protect)
- Platform(s) Employed: VIPER 21/22 (F-16C DCA), RAZOR 31 (F-35A DCA), SENTINEL 11/12 (DCA), SENTRY 71/72 (E-3G C2), tankers TEXACO 61/62, SHELL 63, ARCO 64.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 90% (protect/deter objective).
- Functional Impact: Maintained continuous defensive counterair presence with timely intercept geometry; adversary aircraft did not achieve simulated access to defense core. Minor inefficiencies due to comms bandwidth intermittency for data sharing.
- Re-strike Recommendation: NO. Justification: Objective met; continue posture as required, but no “re-strike” applies.

2.6. DENY ADVERSARY ISR AIRCRAFT ACCESS TO DEFENSE CORE (SIM) – AIR
- Platform(s) Employed: DCA packages (VIPER 21/22, RAZOR 31, SENTINEL 11/12), SENTRY 71/72; escort packages PANTHER 11/12 as protective counterair where required.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 85% (deny/intercept objective).
- Functional Impact: Adversary ISR attempts assessed deterred/turned away in the scenario construct; friendly intercept posture credible. Adversary likely used overhead collection and passive measures as substitute.
- Re-strike Recommendation: NO. Justification: Continue DCA scheduling; focus next cycle on reducing friendly detectability to overhead collection (EMCON discipline, track variability).

2.7. PRIORITY HVA COVERAGE (SIM) – LOGISTICS (Protect/Deter)
- Platform(s) Employed: VIPER 99 (alert), DCA packages, SENTRY 71/72; tanker support ensured endurance.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 90% (protect/deter objective).
- Functional Impact: Alert posture credible; simulated response timelines within required thresholds. No confirmed adversary probing into HVA coverage bubbles beyond standoff.
- Re-strike Recommendation: NO. Justification: Maintain; optimize sortie allocation to sustain over time.

2.8. NAVAL CAP OVER CSG OPERATING AREA (SIM) – NAVAL (Screen/Detect)
- Platform(s) Employed: EAGLE 41 (F/A-18E×4 DCA), HAMMER 51/52 (F/A-18E×4 patrol), GUARDIAN 91 (reserve), SENTRY 71/72 for air picture integration.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 80% (screen/detect objective).
- Functional Impact: Maintained CAP screen; air picture remained stable. Primary risk remains adversary long-range cueing from coastal sensors and overhead ISR rather than direct air penetration.
- Re-strike Recommendation: NO. Justification: Objective met; adjust tactics to complicate adversary targeting (variable altitudes, timing, emissions).

2.9. DETECT/REPORT ADV SURFACE ACTION GROUP RED FLOT-1 (SIM) – NAVAL
- Platform(s) Employed: HAMMER 51/52, BLADE 31; space ISR/SAR support; limited correlation from ELINT due to adversary EMCON.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 40% (detect/report objective progress).
- Functional Impact: Indications of surface activity were obtained, but the track was not maintained at targetable fidelity; assessed adversary maneuvered under EMCON and exploited clutter/weather to reduce detectability.
- Re-strike Recommendation: YES (ISR). Justification: SAG detection is a high-payoff indicator and a potential threat vector; requires expanded search plan, more dwell, and tighter space-air-surface cue integration.

2.10. PASSIVE DETECTION OF MARITIME AIR DEFENSE EMITTERS (SIM) – AIR_DEFENSE
- Platform(s) Employed: F-35A (FALCON 61, RAZOR 31, SENTINEL 12) passive sensing; F/A-18E ESM support; RC-135V for standoff ELINT.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 60% (detect/report objective progress).
- Functional Impact: Improved library entries and rough localization of several maritime air defense-related emissions; incomplete attribution to specific hulls vs coastal nodes.
- Re-strike Recommendation: YES (ISR). Justification: Attribution and continuity are required to enable future defensive planning and to support maritime strike decision timelines if escalated.

2.11. RED SA-XX BATTERY SET (SIM) – AIR_DEFENSE (Desired: Degrade)
- Platform(s) Employed: KNIGHT 11 (F-35A×4 OCA/SEAD) with KNIGHT 12 (F-16C×4 escort) in support; ISR support from RIVET 31/32 and F-35 passive sensing; C2 via SENTRY 71/72.
- Estimated Damage/Effect Achieved: 35% functional degradation (localized/temporary). Physical damage: 0% confirmed.
- Functional Impact: Assessed reduction in engagement efficiency and confidence through simulated SEAD effects: constrained radar emissions, forced mobility/relocation drills, and reduced timeline for adversary track-quality generation during the window. Battery remains operational and capable after the event; degradation not persistent without follow-on pressure.
- Re-strike Recommendation: YES (non-kinetic/ISR; kinetic only upon escalation authority). Justification: Battery is a key access-denial node; present effect is temporary. Next cycle should prioritize precise geolocation of battery components (radar, launcher set, command vehicle) and confirm reload/alternate positions to enable rapid transition to decisive options if hostilities commence.

3. MISSION EFFECTIVENESS ANALYSIS

3.1. Sortie Accounting (Fragged vs Executed vs Effective).
- Sorties/Packages Fragged: 26 mission lines (total aircraft sorties: 60).
- Executed: 25/26 mission lines executed as planned (58/60 aircraft sorties). Two aircraft sorties assessed NMC/aborted (one F-16C from training/continuation and one F/A-18E within a patrol package) with remaining elements completing coverage.
- Effective (met primary objective without major shortfall): 22/25 executed mission lines (approx. 88% of executed). Shortfalls primarily affected maritime detection continuity and comms-enabled cross-cue timing rather than DCA deterrence.

3.2. Weapons Effectiveness Rate.
- Kinetic Ordnance Expended: None (Phase 0).
- Simulated SEAD/EA Effects: Applied during KNIGHT 11 window; assessed moderate short-term impact (reflected in SA-XX functional degradation estimate). Because effects were non-kinetic/simulated, a conventional probability-of-kill metric is not applicable. Effectiveness is assessed by adversary emission behavior change and temporary reduction in track-quality generation (moderate confidence).

3.3. ISR Effectiveness and PED Timeliness.
- SIGINT/ELINT collection was strong against intermittently emitting targets (coastal radars, IADS sector nodes) when adversary radiated. Timeliness of fused reporting was intermittently constrained by degraded wideband relays (TDRS-12/13 degraded; multiple WGS nodes degraded). Protected SATCOM remained available for essential C2.
- Maritime domain awareness gains were incremental; adversary EMCON and maneuver, plus sensor attribution challenges, reduced confidence in clustering and hull-specific identification.

3.4. Intelligence Gaps Identified (Priority).
a. RED SHIELD-N: Precise sector boundaries; mobile radar movement corridors; identification of decoys and alternate emitters; linkage between sector nodes and higher C2.
b. RED SKY-3: Confirmation of alternate site(s) and handoff logic; radar downtime patterns; maintenance/crew cycle indicators.
c. RED NET-A: Node hierarchy, routing paths, redundancy, and identifying key chokepoints; correlation of comms surges to specific operational behaviors (CAP launches, maritime movements).
d. Maritime: Attribution of “RED WAVE-2” emitters (coastal vs embarked); persistent track on “RED FLOT-1;” identification of maritime air defense emitters by platform class.
e. Overhead threat: Adversary likely maintained continuous overhead collection (SAR/EO/ELINT) and may have derived friendly tanker/CAP patterns. Need refined OPSEC and deception plan to protect force posture indicators.

4. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR NEXT CYCLE (DAY 2)

4.1. Priority Re-strikes / Follow-on Actions (Non-kinetic ISR focus unless escalation authority changes).
1) RED SA-XX BATTERY SET: Repeat collection and simulated pressure to force emissions and movement; prioritize component-level geolocation, confirm alternate hides, and observe reload logistics. Objective: raise target solution fidelity and sustain degradation if required.
2) RED NET-A: Expand SIGINT dwell and correlation across time; prioritize identification of node hierarchy and redundancy. Consider synchronized collection windows with adversary expected shift changes and known exercise rhythms.
3) RED FLOT-1 / RED WAVE-2: Increase maritime search continuity using layered collection (airborne ESM + space SAR/EO + passive cues). Prioritize track continuity over single-pass classification.

4.2. Targets Recommended for Removal from JIPTL (Sufficiently Degraded).
- None recommended for removal based on Day 1. Phase 0 produced primarily characterization effects; no target set achieved persistent functional denial/destruction. HVA/CSG defensive coverage objectives were met, but these are not JIPTL “degrade/destroy” targets and should remain as standing defensive tasks rather than removal candidates.

4.3. New Targets Nominated (Based on Observed Adversary Response).
a. IADS Mobility/Support Nodes (New): Identify and nominate suspected SA-XX support elements (reload vehicles, maintenance/support convoy patterns, mobile power units) observed/assessed during the SEAD rehearsal window. Rationale: these nodes are often less defended and enable sustained battery operations.
b. Alternate/Backup Radar Sites (New): Nominate probable alternate early warning radar positions supporting RED SKY-3 continuity (e.g., secondary coastal nodes that assumed coverage during primary silence). Rationale: adversary demonstrated handoff behavior suggesting redundancy.
c. Communications Relay/Bridging Nodes (New): Nominate suspected relay nodes or gateway links enabling RED NET-A resilience (microwave relay chains, SATCOM bridging points, coastal relay hubs). Rationale: observed traffic reroutes imply preplanned alternate paths.
d. Maritime Passive Sensor/Cueing Nodes (New): Nominate suspected passive RF/EO cueing sources near maritime operating areas that may be feeding RED WAVE-2/RED FLOT-1 targeting. Rationale: adversary EMCON indicates reliance on offboard cueing.

4.4. Force/Collection Management Recommendations.
- Adjust CAP/tanker timing and routes to reduce pattern predictability against adversary overhead ISR. Implement stricter emission control where feasible; minimize non-essential radar and datalink transmissions during known overhead windows.
- Increase cross-cue discipline: schedule deliberate “collection windows” where multiple platforms (RC-135, F-35 passive, F/A-18 ESM) are synchronized to exploit brief adversary emissions.
- Mitigate SATCOM bandwidth limitations by prioritizing essential tracks and emitter reports; defer bulk data transfers to optimal relay availability; use protected SATCOM for time-critical C2 and minimal necessary PED summaries.
- Expand PED fusion for maritime attribution by formalizing correlation between ELINT hits, SAR detections, and tactical air picture anomalies; prioritize maintaining a continuous track on one high-value maritime problem set (RED FLOT-1) rather than broad, shallow coverage.

ASSESSMENT CONFIDENCE SUMMARY:
- High confidence: Friendly DCA/CSG deterrence objectives met; no kinetic effects; presence posture credible.
- Moderate confidence: RED SKY-3 and portions of RED SHIELD-N characterization; SA-XX temporary functional degradation.
- Low-to-moderate confidence: RED WAVE-2 clustering and RED FLOT-1 detection/track continuity; RED NET-A hierarchy beyond initial identification.

END OF REPORT.
